items.title: Netherlands demands hundreds of billions in EU budget cuts
items.summary: The Dutch government has co-signed a letter to the EU presidency demanding the bloc’s next budget, which is set every...
items.body_text:
Netherlands demands hundreds of billions in EU budget cuts
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Dutch government has co-signed a letter to the EU presidency demanding the bloc’s next budget, which is set every seven years, be dramatically scaled back.
Prime minister Rob Jetten’s minority coalition is one of six so-called “frugal” governments, whose countries pay more into the EU budget than they get back.
The European Commission has proposed an almost €2 trillion budget for the 2028-2034 period, which governs spending on everything from agriculture to defence and funding for poorer regions.
Along with Germany, Sweden, Denmark, Austria, and Finland, the Netherlands is now pressing for a cut of several hundred billion euros from the proposals.
The letter, which has not been made public but has been seen by major news outlets, states: “Our six countries alone finance almost 40% of all Member States’ contributions. While net contributors as a whole are in the minority, they shoulder around three-quarters of the total financing burden.”
An almost €2 trillion budget would represent a 60% nominal increase in the size of the current budget, which, they argue, is “simply not realistic.”
Divisions
 There are 17 other countries, including Spain and Italy, who are insisting on protections for impoverished regions and struggling sectors like agriculture, and want the overall budget raised above €2 trillion.
The Commission has also suggested creating new EU-wide taxes, including a levy on large companies and a tobacco excise duty, to raise capital and ease the burden on countries like the Netherlands. In June, the Cypriot presidency proposed a 2% cut to the Commission’s plan, which the six considered far too small.
Negotiators want to get a deal done by the end of the year, before elections in France, Italy, Spain and Poland complicate the talks. All 27 member states must agree to the budget.
But according to the Financial Times, a diplomat from one of the six countries said there would be no deal this year unless the budget was cut by hundreds of billions of euros.
Ireland, which currently holds the rotating EU presidency, is due to present a new compromise text in the coming days, ahead of a summit of EU leaders on October 15 and 16. European Council president António Costa will meet Jetten in the Netherlands on October 9 to discuss the budget.
Jetten’s shift
 The letter marks a U-turn for Jetten, whose D66 party went into the 2025 election calling for a European budget twice its current size, financed by new EU-level taxes. The same manifesto proposed €750 to €800 billion a year in extra European investment, paid for with joint borrowing.
In office with his minority coalition, Jetten has taken a different line. At an informal EU summit in Cyprus in April, he rejected the €2 trillion proposal, telling reporters the Dutch contribution would “explode” under the plan, according to De Telegraaf. In June he told NOS the Commission’s proposal was “simply not good enough”.
A big part of the reason is money – at the moment, the Netherlands gets a discount on its EU bill. Brussels wants to end that discount, which would cost the Dutch around €2 billion more a year. In total, the plans would add up to €5.4 billion a year to what the Netherlands pays the EU, according to the Court of Audit, the government’s spending watchdog.

items.title: Five things every first-time buyer in the Netherlands must know
items.summary: Buying your first home is one of the biggest financial decisions most people make in their lives. And as an...
items.body_text:
Partner content
Five things every first-time buyer in the Netherlands must know
Buying your first home is one of the biggest financial decisions most people make in their lives. And as an international in the Netherlands, it’s likely that the process, language and unwritten rules are all different from what you might expect.
Cherene Kruger, founder of Homes for Expats, has spent years helping international buyers through their first Dutch house purchase, and her starting point is always the same: don’t assume the process works the way it does back home.
“The biggest problem is you don’t know what you don’t know,” she says. “You’re not shopping for property on your home turf, which already makes things stressful.” In the Netherlands, that unfamiliar cast list includes two makelaars (estate agents), a bank, a mortgage adviser and a notary: roles that may not exist, or might work quite differently, elsewhere.
The estate agent isn’t on your side
 The most important thing to understand, says Cherene, is who actually represents whom. “The selling makelaar represents the seller. If you appoint a buying makelaar, they are the one representing your interests and fighting in your corner.”
 “I once had a client who kept saying out loud how much she was prepared to pay for a house, right in front of the selling agent,” she says.
It’s a distinction that doesn’t occur to a lot of first-time buyers, and one whose consequences Cherene has experienced herself. She once bought a new-build property that didn’t automatically come with plastered and painted walls, a paved driveway or a levelled garden with grass, because no one had properly explained what was and wasn’t included beforehand.
Don’t get caught up in overbidding
 While overbidding is often a fact of life in the Dutch market, knowing how much to offer can be one of the hardest things for international buyers to navigate. The asking price doesn’t reflect market value, and simply offering more isn’t always the right decision.
Cherene also sees more buyers turning to AI for answers. “AI can be a useful research tool, but it cannot replace someone being on the ground, seeing the property, understanding what’s happening in that particular market and having actual lived experience.”
Cherene’s own approach is deliberately pragmatic: research the area, weigh market value against what a property is actually worth, and look at comparable sales, understand the market value and then decide what the property is worth to you as a buyer. “My job is to help you make the right decision and the right investment,” she says. “You’re buying a house, not a hamburger, so it’s incredibly important we get this right!” She would rather see a client lose a property than win one at a cost that leaves them in negative equity for years to come.
Get financing sorted before you fall for a house
 Every offer Cherene puts together includes two standard conditions: a financing clause and a technical inspection. Both protect the buyer. If financing falls through without a financing condition, the buyer could face a penalty of 10% of the purchase price. A technical inspection condition offers protection if serious defects are uncovered.
For instance, the inspection can unearth problems like hidden mould or rotten beams that aren’t obvious during a viewing. “If there’s a major issue that is going to cost my clients a lot of money, I would rather walk away from a bad relationship than marry just for the sake of getting married.” Depending on how the technical inspection condition has been agreed, serious defects may give the buyer the opportunity to renegotiate or withdraw from the purchase.
For buyers relocating for work, getting that financial picture in order early is arguably the single most useful thing they can do. items.title: Poland recovers looted painting that once hung in SS officers’ club in occupied Warsaw
items.summary: The owner of the painting has donated it to Warsaw's National Museum after learning of its provenance.

A Polish painting looted by Nazi Germany during World War Two, and which once hung in an SS officers’ club, has been returned by its owner, who donated it to the National Museum in Warsaw.
“History is coming home,” said culture minister Marta Cienkowska, celebrating the return of Alfred Wierusz-Kowalski’s Winter – Napoleon’s Retreat from Moscow, which she described as “one of the most significant wartime losses in Polish painting”.
Her ministry is responsible for seeking the return of tens of thousands of artworks and other cultural items that were looted during the war and remain missing.
Kolejny sukces restytucyjny! Odzyskaliśmy jedną z cenniejszych i najbardziej znanych strat wojennych malarstwa polskiego. Obraz „Zima – Odwrót Napoleona spod Moskwy” Alfreda Wierusza-Kowalskiego trafił dziś do zbiorów Muzeum Narodowego w Warszawie.
To efekt naszej współpracy z… pic.twitter.com/Y0wDIBgIGG
— Ministerstwo Kultury i Dziedzictwa Narodowego (@kultura_gov_pl) September 28, 2026
Wierusz-Kowalski, who was active in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, was a renowned realist painter whose work often featured animals alongside people. His Winter – Napoleon’s Retreat from Moscow had, by the 1930s, become part of the collection of Andrzej Rotwand, a wealthy banker and industrialist.
In June 1939, it was featured in an exhibition organised by the Society for the Encouragement of Fine Arts in Warsaw, which occupied the building that is now the famous Zachęta National Gallery of Art.
However, the exhibition was brought to an abrupt end when Nazi Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939. The works on display, along with other items from the gallery, were seized by the occupiers, with many used to decorate the offices and apartments of German officials.
Winter – Napoleon’s Retreat from Moscow was displayed in a club for high-ranking SS and police officers located in Warsaw’s Blanka Palace. The same building also housed Warsaw’s German-installed commissioner, Helmut Otto, and mayor, Ludwig Leist.
No information has been released as to the fate of the painting in the immediate aftermath of the war. However, it eventually came into the possession of Ewa Tsonis, who has now handed it back.
Speaking at a ceremony in the National Museum in Warsaw, Tsonis said that her late father, Michał Stefan Koryzna, had purchased the painting in the 1960s from Desa, a major gallery and auction house, in the city of Kraków.
“I grew up with this painting. It was greatly appreciated and loved in our family,” she said. However, after recently conducting research into the painting’s history, she became aware of its provenance and notified the culture ministry.
Experts from the National Museum in Warsaw confirmed the identity of the painting, which remains in good condition and in its original frame. Tsonis then donated the work to the museum.
“Restitution is not possible without the cooperation of many people and institutions – both on the side of the state and on the part of the owners of the works,” said Cienkowska, who thanked Tsonis for her “incredibly responsible and civic-minded attitude”.
“Such attitudes are still rare but, because we constantly talk about restitution – we search for lost works and strive to recover them – we are increasingly approached by people who own lost objects and feel a sense of responsibility for cultural heritage.”
Cienkowska noted that the culture ministry has so far secured the return of over 920 works, with around 200 more restitution cases currently underway in 18 countries.

items.title: Poland changes rules of engagement for firing on foreign aircraft amid growing Russia threat
items.summary: Visual identification of targets will no longer be required.
items.body_text:
Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Poland is changing the procedures under which its military can fire upon foreign aircraft, citing the “growing threat from Russia”. Visual identification of targets will no longer be required, with other forms of data to be used instead.
The move follows a series of violations of Polish airspace over the last year by Russian drones, a missile and a helicopter, as well as Russia’s increasing use of jet-powered drones to attack targets in Ukraine close to the Polish border.
Polska zmienia procedury użycia uzbrojenia dla lotnictwa w przypadku zwalczania obcych statków powietrznych. To wnioski Dowódcy Operacyjnego generała Ireneusza Nowaka z ostatnich tygodni.
To także odpowiedź na rosnące zagrożenie ze strony Rosji, doświadczenia wojny w Ukrainie…
— Cezary Tomczyk (@CTomczyk) September 28, 2026
“In the coming days, the defence minister will change the procedures for firing by Polish planes and helicopters at objects flying to us from the direction of Russia,” announced deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk on Monday, quoted by news service Defence24.
The change, as Tomczyk explained in a statement later issued on social media, will shift requirements away from requiring visual identification of foreign aerial objects and towards so-called “positive identification”.
The latter involves identifying an object based on a combination of several other, non-visual sources of information, such as using radar and other sensors to determine its speed, altitude, trajectory and flight parameters, as well as a lack of IFF (identification friend or foe) from an object.
Tomczyk said that the change was being made based on the “conclusions from recent weeks” made by the operational commander of Poland’s armed forces, General Ireneusz Nowak.
It is a “response to the growing threat from Russia, experiences from the war in Ukraine, and the emergence of new air attack means – primarily fast jet drones and cruise missiles in the case of which the time for reaction is very brief”, added Tomczyk.
The minister said that positive identification would only be issued when there is a “sufficiently high degree of certainty in determining what we are dealing with”. He noted that accurate target identification is particularly crucial in peacetime, when there are civilian aircraft in Polish airspace.
The change will mean “not less identification, but a different way of conducting it: faster and based on data from multiple sources”.
Poland's government has issued public guidance on how to act in the case of airborne attacks, amid growing concerns over the threat from Russia.
It is also preparing evacuation plans and clearer markings for 85,000 shelters across the countryhttps://t.co/vMEMU6mlRx
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 25, 2026
Defence24 reports that the government, military and many experts have found current rules of engagement to be overly restrictive and not suited to meeting the scale and type of threat facing Poland today.
It points to last week’s violation of Polish airspace by a Russian helicopter, which crossed the border from Kaliningrad and spent around 42 seconds in Poland before returning.
The website also notes that Russia’s growing use of jet-powered drones, which are able to travel much faster than traditional unmanned aerial vehicles, is a further threat.
Such drones have recently been used to attack targets along the Ukrainian side of the border with Poland, including a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw.

A Belarusian man has been convicted in Poland of preparing an act of sabotage on behalf of foreign intelligence. The 28-year-old, who can be named only as Vitaliy S. under Polish privacy law, was sentenced to three and a half years in prison.
The authorities have not identified which country he was working for. However, Poland has in recent years been a primary target for sabotage carried out by operatives on behalf of Russia, many of whom have been detained, charged and convicted.

In July 2025, Vitaliy S. carried out preparations to undertake sabotage in the form of an arson attack on a warehouse in the eastern Polish city of Chełm, reported broadcaster Radio Zet from his trial. He was paid the equivalent of 1,474 zloty (€337) in cryptocurrency.
According to Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW), he had been recruited via the Telegram messaging service and was tasked with filming the warehouse and sending prepared material about it to his handlers.
Vitaliy S. was detained in August 2025, charged with espionage and then indicted to stand trial in July this year. He had faced up to eight years in prison, but, on the first day of his trial at the regional court in Lublin, accepted a sentence of three and a half years agreed with prosecutors, reports Polskie Radio.
Przed Sądem Okręgowym w Lublinie ruszył proces Białorusina Vitalija S. Ze względu na bezpieczeństwo kraju Sąd wykluczył jawność. 28-latek oskarżony jest o akt dywersji na rzecz obcego wywiadu. Planował podpalić magazyn w Chełmie. Wszystko udaremniła ABW. @RadioZET_NEWS pic.twitter.com/dxhwwJom0f
— Mateusz Kasiak (@mateusz_kasiak) September 28, 2026
Poland has in recent years detained, charged and in some cases convicted dozens of agents accused of carrying out espionage, sabotage and other so-called “hybrid actions” on behalf of Russia and its ally Belarus.
Many such actions have been carried out not by trained operatives sent to Poland, but by so-called “disposable agents”, often immigrants and refugees from Ukraine and Belarus already in Poland, who are hired through Telegram and paid in cryptocurrency to carry out acts of sabotage and espionage.
A report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism published earlier this year found that Poland was the “primary focus” of Russia’s growing campaign of sabotage in Europe.
Poland is the "primary focus" of Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe, finds a new report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism.
Among 151 incidents identified since 2022, 31 of them took place in Poland – more than in any other country https://t.co/QXfSI00FD6
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 3, 2026
Those incidents have included a number of arson attacks, including one that caused Warsaw’s biggest shopping centre to burn down. Recent fires at a drone factory and a satellite internet ground station have also been blamed on Russia.
Last year, two men working on behalf of Russia used explosives in an attempt to derail a train before fleeing across the border into Belarus.

items.title: Belgrade Mayor Denies Punching Opposition Councillor in Street Altercation
items.summary: Ruling party mayor Aleksandar Sapic denies assaulting opposition councillor and breaking her nose and jaw in a street altercation - saying he only defended himself against the woman's husband.
items.body_text:
Belgrade Mayor Denies Punching Opposition Councillor in Street Altercation
Belgrade Mayor Aleksandar Sapic on Tuesday denied physically assaulting an opposition city councillor, Tatjana Micic, the night before, insisting he had “only defended” himself after being verbally attacked.
The Kreni-Promeni (Move-Change) movement said Sapic, a senior official of the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, assaulted their councillor, Micic, and her husband, while they were walking their dog near their home.
The movement said Micic sustained suffered a broken nose and jaw, which it said was confirmed by medical documentation. BIRN could not independently confirm this.
“The Mayor rushed at me, claiming I had brought people outside his home [to hold a protest], and got right in my face. When I took out my phone and tried to film him, he started hitting my arm, and my husband tried to protect me. I stepped between the two of them to prevent things from getting out of hand, when he [Sapic] hit me on the nose,” Micic told media outlet N1.
A friend called the police, she said, but did not initially say Sapic was involved.
“When they [the police] realised who it was, two more patrols arrived, followed by the head of the New Belgrade [district] police department,” she told N1.
Sapic denied the claims at the press conference on Tuesday, saying he had “always condemned every form of violence”, particularly against women.
“My personal code, as a man and as a human being, has never allowed me to do such a thing, nor would I ever allow myself to do it,” Sapic said.
He said that during his evening walk with a friend, he had encountered “a person who had distributed leaflets, called on people to gather outside my home, gathered people there and, in every possible way, endangered both my safety and my peace”.
When he recognised her, he had asked “why she had been coming to his home”. He claimed he was then verbally attacked, first by the man and then by the woman.
Sapic said he had only defended himself from the woman’s husband.
“I have never attacked anyone first in my life … I believe I acted correctly. I did not touch the woman in question, except that at the moment when he came towards me and they started pushing, I moved her away from me precisely so that I would not come into any kind of contact with her,” he explained.
He said he then went to the police station, where he remained until the early hours, to cogive his accont of the incident.
He said that he was sorry if the woman was injured. “I would like to know how she was injured and who injured her. Because I certainly did not injure her, and that is what I am asking the competent authorities to establish,” he added.
A friend of Sapic also addressed journalists, confirming Sapic’s version of events.
The Prosecutor’s Office said Sapic was released after being questioned and more steps would be taken once the facts were established.
Prime ministerial candidate Aleksandar Vucic, who stepped down as president on Sunday to run in elections scheduled for October 25, said that Sapic “should have stepped away” when the incident happened.
“You hold public office; as a public official, you should have removed yourself from the situation. Cross to the other side of the street if necessary, but you must not take part in something like that. The responsibility lies entirely with Sapic. There is no doubt that there was a provocation, but you cannot respond in that way,” Vucic said.
The Kreni-Promeni movement said it will file a criminal complaint and demand the arrest of Sapic.

items.title: Mayor’s Resignation Deals Fresh Blow to Turkey’s Fragmented Opposition
items.summary: Ankara Mayor Mansur Yavas’ resignation from the Republican People’s Party has worsened the embattled opposition’s plight ahead of the next elections – potentially benefitting Turkey’s authoritarian president.
items.body_text:
Ankara Mayor Mansur Yavas’ resignation from the Republican People’s Party, CHP, has further fragmented Turkey’s opposition, leaving open the political future of one of the few figures who polls suggest could mount a strong challenge to President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Yavas on September 23 announced that he was leaving the CHP following months of turmoil that have split the party between the leadership, restored to Kemal Kilicdaroglu, and the New Party, Turkey’s new main opposition party, established by former CHP leader Ozgur Ozel.
“I am resigning my membership of the CHP and will continue my political path as an independent,” Yavas said, adding that the decision followed a period of legal and political disputes that had deeply divided the opposition.
The decision leaves Yavas outside both major camps that emerged from the CHP’s crisis. It also raises a larger question for an already fractured opposition: whether the Ankara Mayor is gradually withdrawing from national politics – or positioning himself as an independent figure who could eventually unite different opposition constituencies.

items.title: Powerful, Plugged-in, Predatory: Czech Arms Maker CSG Cashes in on West’s Rearmament
items.summary: Led by the country’s wealthiest man, Czechoslovak Group regularly makes the headlines for bumper profits, hushed-up disputes and aggressive business practices.
items.body_text:
One figure has pulled ahead of the rest of the Czech Republic’s chasing wealthy pack. With a fortune of 470 billion crowns (over 19 billion euros), the 34-year-old owner and CEO of Czechoslovak Group (CSG), Michal Strnad, saw his wealth increase by 40 per cent in a single year, according to the rich list published by Euro.cz at the end of August.
Only the energy magnate and global investor Daniel Kretinsky appears to be keeping up, coming in second with a fortune of 432 billion crowns. In third place was PPF heiress Renata Kellnerova with 385 billion crowns.
It is, however, a highly volatile numbers game, with most of Strnad’s wealth tied up in his 85 per cent stake in CSG, Czechia’s leading arms manufacturer. And it’s been a chaotic, roller-coaster year for the defence group, with CSG shares losing about 60 per cent of their value between its record-breaking January IPO on the Amsterdam Stock Exchange and June, before recouping some of its losses since.
CSG’s volatile stock is only one of several recent setbacks experienced by the conglomerate this past year, after facing allegations of industrial property theft, suspicions of inflating production capacity figures, and increased scrutiny over its ties to top political figures, especially in Slovakia and Czechia – all of course denied by CSG.
BIRN spoke to several sources who’ve had dealings with the group and its top management, but prefer to remain anonymous in order to speak candidly.
A major European player
After going public at the start of 2026, CSG could boast of having orchestrated the largest defence IPO in history and became the most valuable publicly listed company in Central Europe, surpassing Czech state-controlled utility CEZ and Polish oil giant Orlen.
“CSG’s listing on the Amsterdam Stock Exchange represents a milestone not only for the company itself, but also for the Czech [defence] industry as a whole,” market analyst Jean-Paul van Oudheusden told Seznam Zpravy, echoing the industry-wide excitement that anticipated and followed the company’s 15 per cent stock offering.
However, Vladimir Snidl, who has been covering CSG for years for the Slovak daily Dennik N, tells BIRN that “it’s not a black-and-white story.” He argues that while CSG “profits from very unfair types of public procurements”, the Prague-based group’s pro-Ukraine leanings as well as its economic, industrial and fiscal added-value in the countries where it operates – especially Czechia and Slovakia – paint a more complex picture of the arms maker.
Founded in the 1990s by Jaroslav Strnad, Michal’s father, under the name Excalibur Army, a small company trading in discarded military equipment, CSG has grown in scope, positioning itself as a key ammunition supplier to Ukraine and NATO allies, riding the waves of European rearmament, and capitalising on the mounting sense of geopolitical doom.
“They have truly built something that is probably unparalleled in the post-revolutionary history of the Czech Republic and Slovakia – a true arms empire that today rivals even the largest European giants in the industrial sector,” highlights Snidl.
The group is now believed to be the world’s largest producer of small-calibre ammunition and Europe’s second top producer of medium- and large-calibre ammo after Germany’s Rheinmetall.
It has about 40 production plants in nine countries (Czechia, Slovakia, Germany, Serbia, Italy, Spain, the UK, India and the US), employs 14,000 people, and saw its net profit increase by over 35 per cent in 2025, with preliminary 2026 results continuing in the double digits.
“We see CSG, together with Rheinmetall, as the most dynamic growth story in the entire defence sector” for the 2025-2030 period, said Patria Finance analyst Michal Krikava.
Emblematic of this optimism, barely a week goes by without CSG announcing new multi-million arms deals, armament joint-ventures and major acquisitions – either from the conglomerate itself or its majority owner: from acquiring a minority stake

items.body_text:
The more than HUF 4 billion project included campus renovations and new digital equipment.Continue reading
More than 16,000 freshmen are beginning their higher education studies this year at Babes-Bolyai University (BBTE) in Cluj-Napoca (Kolozsvár), of whom nearly 2,200 are enrolled in Hungarian-language programs, Maszol.ro reported on Monday.
Among the students enrolled in Hungarian-language programs, 1,579 are studying in full-time or distance-learning undergraduate programs, while 577 are beginning master’s programs. In the bachelor’s program, 46 percent of first-year students enrolled in tuition-based spots, while in the master’s program, approximately 30 percent of students were admitted to tuition-based spots.
At the university’s opening ceremony, Rector Daniel David emphasized that BBTE is one of Eastern Europe’s most significant centers of higher education and its most complex multicultural institution. He pointed out that,
reflecting the history of Transylvania and the institution, Hungarian and German are considered official languages at the university alongside Romanian.
According to the rector, BBTE’s identity is built on the importance of science, culture, and innovation. Daniel David described the university as a “bastion of scientific truth and democracy” in an era in which pseudosciences and anti-democratic movements pose a serious challenge to society.
Bálint Markó, the vice rector responsible for the Hungarian division, emphasized that, in light of the PISA results, the university must simultaneously respond constructively to shortcomings and preserve intellectual freedom in order to launch new, forward-looking programs. He stated that the educational institution must strive to respond to societal needs, while at the same time holding fast to certain programs that it must not abandon, even if they seem unnecessary.
We must be free in our thoughts and initiatives, and we must pass this on to our students and to society. These must be the guiding principles for the university and for the operation and development of the Hungarian department,”
Maszol quoted the vice rector as saying in his speech delivered in Hungarian.
According to information from the university’s communications office, the dual-major programs launched last year have lived up to expectations. A sufficient number of applicants were admitted to the Hungarian Language and Literature–Folklore, Mathematics–Computer Science, Physics–Computer Science, and Philosophy–Art History programs, meaning that classes will begin this fall for all dual-major programs.
Starting this academic year, the Hungarian-language undergraduate program in Public Administration will resume in a distance learning format at the BBTE’s branch campus in Sfantu-Gheorghe (Sepsiszentgyörgy); this program attracted significant interest during the fall admissions cycle, with nearly twice as many applicants as available spots.
This summer, BBTE obtained the necessary permits to launch a doctoral program in medicine. The doctoral program will begin in the fall of 2026, and prospective doctoral students will have the opportunity to work with a Hungarian-speaking doctoral advisor, the university announced.

items.body_text:
The rights of everyone are inviolable in Europe, except those of Christians.Continue reading
The Axioma Center for Persecuted Christians (CPC) recently began operations under the leadership of former State Secretary for the help for Persecuted Christians, Tristan Azbej. Its aim is to carry on the intellectual legacy of Hungary’s previous engagement regarding persecuted Christians, following the new TISZA administration’s decision to dissolve that government unit, reported Magyar Nemzet.
As a new international mission of the Axioma Center aims to ensure that often-forgotten Christian communities—which endure great hardship—are not left to fend for themselves; it seeks to ensure their cries for help are heard in the Western world and that they receive tangible assistance.
The center maintains that the dissolution of the Hungarian government’s state secretariat responsible for aiding persecuted Christians must not result in a lack of support for those Christians who continue to rely on Hungary to secure their communities’ future. It is the obligation of every Western nation to engage in international aid activities.
Under the Viktor Orbán government, Hungary decided to direct this assistance to the world’s most persecuted religious community—Christians—serving for a long time as the sole provider of such aid and setting an example for other nations with a Christian heritage.
Since its inception in 2016, the government unit responsible for aiding persecuted Christians—a state secretariat that was dissolved following the April elections—has channeled assistance and support from the Hungarian people to Christians persecuted for their faith or living in crisis zones across more than sixty countries.
This government unit ceased operations in May; although the new government promised to continue supporting persecuted Christians, the exact opposite has occurred over the past four or five months.

He added that this is why they considered it vital to preserve this intellectual legacy. They are continuing their work on behalf of persecuted Christians not through a government program, but within a civil society framework. “This is not merely about preserving a legacy. We feel it is a moral obligation, too, because
aiding persecuted Christians has become a national vocation for Hungary—a mission that must not be interrupted,”
Azbej added.

On October 1, the 19th District will transform into a musical stage, with performances taking place at key locations, squares, streets, and shopping centers in Kispest, organized by the KMO Cultural Center and the László Szatmári Elementary School of the Arts. The program includes
a brass band flash mob and a concert at KÖKI, a rolling piano, Irish folk music in front of the Kispesti Centrum Department Store, a cello concert at the Wekerle Music Pavilion, and performances by local musicians at the Kispesti Kertvárosi Community Center.
Surprise concerts will be held at the Jókai Mór Cultural Center in Budaörs and other venues, a Joni Mitchell tribute night at the József Attila Cultural Center in Dorog, and wind ensemble performances and cultural programs at the Agóra Promenade in Szekszárd and the Mihály Babits Cultural Center. A memorial ceremony combined with a wreath-laying will be held at the Veszprém Pantheon, featuring the Veszprém City Mixed Choir.
At the University of Szeged’s Béla Bartók Faculty of Arts, mini-concerts will be held during the day, followed by a concert featuring faculty and students in the evening; in the afternoon, a trombone concert will be performed from the balcony of the Reök Palace.
KULT7 will host a Bartók concert by the Péter Sárik Trio; the program also features free programs at the House of Music, lunchtime concerts featuring the Era Nova String Quartet, a performance by the Zádor Trio, and a screening of Bereményi and Másik’s film Háború van (War Is On). A György Czigány Salon will be inaugurated on World Music Day at the Óbuda Social Club, from where Bartók Radio will broadcast the program Muzsikáló délután live starting at 3:00 p.m., followed by Ádám Bősze’s program Levéláriák.
Ferenc Liszt’s symphonic poem Les Préludes, as well as Béla Bartók’s Piano Concerto No. 3 and his Concerto for Orchestra, will be performed at the MÁV Symphony Orchestra’s Friday concert—held in celebration of World Music Day—at the Academy of Music, featuring pianist Zoltán Fejérvári.

items.body_text:
Czech Study Finds Supporting Homeless People Can Save Public Money
Prague Morning
A Czech experiment in which homeless people received CZK 100,000 with no conditions attached suggests that early financial support can reduce some of the costs associated with homelessness.
The project, known as New Leaf, was carried out by the Czech organization Neposeda in cooperation with researchers from Charles University.
The findings indicate that the state spends an average of about CZK 200,000 a year on each person experiencing homelessness, with healthcare, social services and police work accounting for a significant share of the total.
The researchers concluded that leaving people without support can ultimately be more expensive for public finances than providing targeted assistance.
How the New Leaf experiment worked
The project ran from summer 2024 until the end of 2025 and was inspired by a similar initiative in Canada.
Researchers focused on people who had been living on the streets for no more than two and a half years. The aim was to examine whether intervention at an earlier stage of homelessness could prevent longer-term problems.
Participants were divided into several groups. Forty people received CZK 100,000 without restrictions on how the money could be used. Another 20 were offered the support of a personal social worker instead, while 40 people formed a control group and received no additional assistance.
The study initially involved 100 people. One participant died from a serious illness shortly after the project began, leaving 99 participants in the final research sample.
The researchers tracked participants’ use of public services and their contact with state authorities, including emergency medical services, hospitals, outpatient healthcare, social services and police.
Healthcare accounts for the largest share
The study estimates that the state spends around CZK 200,000 annually on each homeless person.
Healthcare represented almost 43% of the estimated expenditure. Low-threshold services, which provide basic support and a safe place for people experiencing homelessness, accounted for around a quarter of the total.
Police work represented another 9%, or more than 18,000 crowns per person each year.
The wider cost to public finances
Data from the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs recorded 11,641 homeless people in the Czech Republic in the previous year.
Based on the estimated annual cost per person, direct public expenditure associated with homelessness amounts to roughly 2.33 billion crowns a year.

items.body_text:
Smartwings Cuts Prague Flights as Winter Schedule Shrinks
Prague Morning
Smartwings is reducing its winter flight schedule from Prague, with several routes being cancelled, frequencies cut and new connections postponed until spring 2027.
The biggest changes will affect Spain, a popular choice for Czech travelers looking for warmer weather during the autumn and winter months.
The airline will suspend flights between Prague and Valencia from November 2 until the beginning of March.
Flights to several other Spanish destinations will also be reduced. Smartwings will cut its Málaga service from two flights a day to one, while Barcelona will move from daily flights to four to six services a week.
Flights to Mallorca will be reduced from four per week to two. The Prague–Madrid route will continue, but flights will operate on an irregular schedule.
Smartwings is also suspending flights from Prague to Nice until early March.
New Prague routes pushed back
Several routes that were expected to launch this year will now have to wait until spring 2027.
The postponed connections include new services to Venice and Bergen, Norway. Smartwings has also delayed the return of flights to Brussels and Bucharest.
Both Brussels and Bucharest were suspended in the spring, with Smartwings originally planning to restore the routes in October.
Eurowings also reduces Prague services
Eurowings is making changes to its Prague schedule as well. The German carrier has cancelled its planned winter flights to Madeira, Portugal.
The route had been scheduled to return for the winter season, but Eurowings will instead offer tickets to Madeira through a partnership with Smartwings, which continues to operate flights to the Portuguese island.
Eurowings will also suspend its Prague–Stockholm service for most of January.
Higher fuel costs affect airline schedules
The changes come as airlines face higher operating costs linked to fuel prices.
According to Eurocontrol, the European organization responsible for coordinating air traffic management, jet fuel prices in Europe more than doubled between the beginning of the year and mid-September.
Airlines around the world have been adjusting schedules as fuel costs fluctuate amid the conflict in the Middle East. Route cancellations and reduced frequencies are among the measures carriers are using to adapt to changing market conditions.

items.body_text:
Home Baking Returns to Czech Kitchens as Flour Sales Rise
Prague Morning
Home baking is gaining momentum in the Czech Republic, with online supermarket Rohlik.cz reporting a sharp increase in demand for baking ingredients this year.
Flour has been at the center of the trend. Sales of organic flour have risen by almost 72 percent compared with the previous year, while conventional flour sales increased by around 23 percent.
The change has also affected the balance of sales. Organic flour previously accounted for about 19 percent of flour purchases at Rohlik.cz. That figure has now climbed to almost 25 percent.
The figures suggest that customers are not simply buying more flour but are also paying greater attention to the type and quality of the ingredients they use.
Rohlik.cz CEO Miroslava Vopatová says baking continues to play a role in family life, particularly as an activity shared across generations. The supermarket has responded by offering products at different price points, from private-label options to organic and farm-produced ingredients.
Yeast sales tell a different story
The increase in demand for flour has not been mirrored by yeast.
Sales of yeast have been gradually falling since the surge in home baking during the coronavirus pandemic. One shift remains noticeable, however: shoppers are increasingly choosing fresh yeast rather than dried yeast.
Home baking in the Czech Republic is also strongly seasonal. Christmas remains the busiest period of the year, while a smaller increase usually occurs in March and April. Demand drops during the summer months.
For experienced bakers, the quality of the final product often depends on relatively simple details. Yeast dough needs enough time and warmth to rise properly, while rushing the process can affect the result.
The preparation of the filling matters as well. Curd cheese should be drained thoroughly before being added to a cake or pastry, reducing the risk of excess moisture making the dough soggy. Fruit fillings should also be sufficiently thick rather than watery.
These practical details can make a noticeable difference, particularly in traditional Czech pastries whose recipes are often passed down through families.

Ketevan Khurodze Approved as New GD MP After Maia Bitadze Becomes Culture Minister
Businesswoman Ketevan Khurodze has been approved as a Georgian Dream MP in the disputed Parliament with the support of 79 lawmakers, replacing Maia Bitadze, who left her parliamentary seat after being appointed culture minister on September 15.
Khurodze was number 105 on the Georgian Dream party list in the 2024 parliamentary elections. According to media reports, she is the director of LLC Meidani Property, a company within the Meidani Group, which operates in the real estate management and development sector. She also serves as director of the LLC Sighnaghi Ethnopark in Georgia’s eastern Kakheti region and owns a 25% stake in LLC Geonut, a company operating in the hazelnut sector.
Khurodze is also the Vice President for Administration and Finance at East-West University, a higher education institution located in Tbilisi. According to the university, she graduated from the Faculty of Law at Tbilisi State University in 2007 and from the Caucasus School of Law at Caucasus University in 2010. She subsequently completed PhD studies in civil law at the Georgian Technical University.
She replaces Bitadze, who had served as an MP since 2020 and chaired the parliamentary Committee on Environmental Protection and Natural Resources. Bitadze was appointed Culture Minister on September 15, replacing Tinatin Rukhadze, who stepped down in July after less than two years in office, citing health reasons.

items.body_text:
‘Over 2,000 South Ossetian Fighters’ Take Part in Ukraine War, Russian Military Official Says
More than 2,000 fighters from the Russian-occupied Tskhinvali region/South Ossetia are taking part in Russia’s war against Ukraine, according to Artem Abramov, a representative of Russia’s 4th Military Base stationed in the occupied region.
Abramov made the statement during a roundtable at the “South Ossetian State University” on September 28, titled “The Role of Russia in Ensuring the International Recognition of South Ossetia.” The event brought together university students and representatives of the Russian military base.
“South Ossetia makes an important contribution to the Russian military operation in Ukraine,” Abramov said, according to the local news agency RES. He said volunteers from the region had fought in [the Ukrainian region of] Donbas since 2014 and that their numbers had since increased significantly. “More than 2,000 fighters from South Ossetia are fighting in the SVO [‘Special Military Operation’] zone,” he said, using Moscow’s term for its full-scale war against Ukraine. Abramov added that many had received Russian military orders and medals.
Abramov also said that what he described as a “victorious” conclusion to the war would have a positive impact on the South Caucasus.
The involvement of volunteers and servicemen from Georgia’s Russian-occupied regions in Russia’s war against Ukraine has been reported since the early weeks of the full-scale invasion. In March 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine alleged Russia was recruiting mercenaries from occupied Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali Region/South Ossetia.
Later that month, it said Russia had transferred about 2,000 troops from the two occupied regions to Ukraine, which also included “South Ossetian” servicemen. Casualties among South Ossetian fighters were also reported in the first months of the invasion.

items.body_text:
Botchorishvili Takes Part in Toronto Conference on Returning Ukrainian Children, Civilians, PoWs
Georgian Dream Foreign Affairs Minister Maka Botchorishvili participated in the Second International Conference on Returning Ukrainian Children, Detained Civilians, and Prisoners of War, held in Toronto, Canada, on September 28-29, and held several bilateral meetings with Canadian officials on the sidelines of the conference.
The conference, co-hosted by Canada, Ukraine and Norway, brought together foreign ministers and senior representatives to strengthen international efforts to bring Ukrainian children, detained civilians and prisoners of war home, protect those remaining under Russian control, and ensure access to rehabilitation and reintegration services for those who return.
On September 29, Botchorishvili held several meetings, including with Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand.
According to the Georgian Foreign Ministry, the meeting with Anand focused on “key areas of bilateral relations between Georgia and Canada,” with particular attention to “Black Sea security issues and the situation in the region.”
The two officials also discussed prospects for strengthening trade and economic ties, while taking into account “Georgia’s role in the Middle Corridor and Canada’s trade diversification policy.”
Botchorishvili also met with Ahmed Hussen, Canada’s Chair of the House of Commons Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs and International Development.
According to the Georgian MFA, the meeting addressed “cooperation between the legislative bodies of the two countries and the important role of the parliamentary dimension in further strengthening bilateral relations,” with particular attention to “prospects for deepening political and trade and economic cooperation.”
Conference on Ukrainian Children, Citizens, PoWs
Addressing the conference, Botchorishvili highlighted the severe humanitarian consequences of the ongoing war against Ukraine, noting that its impact extends beyond the battlefield and requires attention from the international community, according to the Georgian Foreign Ministry.
“The war against Ukraine continues to cause immense suffering to civilians, with consequences extending far beyond the battlefield. The situation of Ukrainian children, detained civilians, and prisoners of war requires our continued and collective attention,” the ministry quoted Botchorishvili as saying.
Botchorishvili also spoke about Georgia’s “own experience,” noting that the consequences of occupation and conflict are “all too familiar to Georgia,” the MFA said.
“Our own experience of conflict and occupation has shown us the long-term humanitarian consequences of war. Russia’s ongoing occupation of Georgia’s two regions has left hundreds of thousands of people displaced from their homes, while denying them the fundamental right to return safely, voluntarily, and with dignity,” Botchorishvili said, according to the MFA.
“We know the pain of displacement, separation from families, and communities torn apart.”
Botchorishvili reaffirmed Georgia’s unwavering support for the sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity of Ukraine within its internationally recognized borders, saying that “Georgia will continue to stand firmly with the Ukrainian people, in support of international law, human dignity, and the principles of the United Nations Charter.”

items.body_text:
Azerbaijan’s state oil company SOCAR is expanding its footprint in Italy beyond oil and gas, entering a long-term partnership with the country’s national football teams and joining efforts to cap fuel prices at its Italian petrol stations.
The moves come as Azerbaijan and Italy seek to deepen economic ties beyond their longstanding energy partnership. SOCAR’s growing presence in Italy follows its acquisition of energy operator Italiana Petroli in 2026. Baku and Rome are also pursuing cooperation in investment, industry, transport, connectivity and technology.
On 26 September, SOCAR and the Italian Football Federation (FIGC) signed an agreement under which the Azerbaijani company will become the global energy partner of Italy’s national football teams from January 2027 until December 2030, with an option to extend the partnership until 2032.
The agreement was signed on the sidelines of the Second Azerbaijan International Investment Forum in Baku.
On 28 September, SOCAR also agreed to match fuel price caps introduced by Italy’s Eni, setting the price of diesel at €2,19 ($2.49) per litre and petrol at €1.99 ($2.26) per litre at participating IP stations. The move came as the Italian government seeks to contain rising fuel costs. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni welcomed the companies’ measures and i also thanked Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev on X for the decision.
Energy continues to form the backbone of Azerbaijan–Italy economic relations. Italy is Azerbaijan’s largest trading partner, with bilateral trade reaching approximately $12 billion in 2025, according to Aliyev.
Azerbaijan exported 25 billion cubic metres of natural gas in 2025, of which 9.5 billion cubic metres went to Italy. The gas is transported through the Trans Adriatic Pipeline (TAP), a key part of the Southern Gas Corridor. Baku and Rome have discussed increasing gas supplies to Italy and further expanding TAP.
Azerbaijan also remains a major supplier of crude oil to Italy. According to Azerbaijan’s Energy Ministry, Italy received 10.34 million tonnes of Azerbaijani oil and 9.5 billion cubic metres of gas in 2025.
As of January 2026, TAP had transported 54.3 billion cubic metres of Azerbaijani gas to Europe, including 45.4 billion cubic metres to Italy.
During Meloni’s visit to Baku in May, Aliyev said the State Oil Fund of Azerbaijan had invested approximately $3 billion in the Italian economy and that the two sides were discussing directing additional investments towards new projects. He also said around 130 Italian companies were operating in Azerbaijan and that Italian companies were involved in 23 projects in Nagorno-Karabakh and Eastern Zangezur.
Meloni said during the visit that an Azerbaijan–Italy business forum was planned for the second half of 2026 in Baku. She said the forum was intended to turn the countries’ political cooperation into concrete opportunities for companies and workers, adding that energy was ‘not the only field’ of cooperation.
The two countries have also identified connectivity as an area for further cooperation. Italy has presented itself as a potential gateway for Azerbaijan to European and Mediterranean markets, while Baku has sought to strengthen its role as a transport and energy link between Europe and Asia.

items.title: Armenia’s ruling party wins municipal elections uncontested
items.summary: The opposition did not widely field candidates in the local elections.
items.body_text:
On Sunday, the Civil Contract party was re-elected in two of the four Armenian communities where municipal elections were held, having run uncontested. The opposition, which had promised to field candidates in the regional elections, did not do so.
In two other communities, the results have yet to be announced.
This fall, 19 areas will hold municipal elections, but the opposition isn’t contesting them widely. Strong Armenia will run only in Stepanavan, while in Hrazdan, Tsakhadzor, Martuni, Araks and Artashat the opposition will be represented by candidates from the Armenia Alliance.
Civil Contract’s candidate for the town of Tumanyan in Armenia’s Lori province, Suren Tumanyan, has been re-elected with 95.1% of the vote. He ran uncontested. In 2021 Tumanyan ran in the local elections on the opposition Republican Party list and defeated Civil Contract. He left the opposition party and joined the ruling party in 2026. He confirmed the move to Factor.am, without explaining why he left the Republican Party.
The ruling Civil Contract party often recruits popular candidates from other parties. In Goris, for example, Mayor Arush Arushanyan, a former vocal critic of the government who accused Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan of losing Nagorno-Karabakh before, will ally with Civil Contract in the next elections.
Prior to the election, Pashinyan announced they would form an electoral alliance with Arushanyan’s Business Party. While Goris voters backed Civil Contract in the 2021 parliamentary election, they elected Arushanyan as mayor in the local vote that same year. Pashinyan said that the decision also reflects a wish to avoid renewed tensions in the community and added that similar ‘solidarity alliances’ could be formed in other communities.
Strong Armenia, the largest opposition force in parliament, won 26% in the Tumanyan community in June but fielded no candidate in its local election. The faction’s secretary, Tigran Abrahamyan, told Factor.am that the party will contest some local elections and skip others, focusing on communities where it sees a high chance of winning.
Tumanyan is the largest of the four communities holding elections, with a population of over 4,000. The council here is elected under the proportional system. Because Civil Contract was the only party standing, voters could only vote ‘for’ or ‘against,’ which meant the party needed more than half of the votes cast, with no minimum turnout thresholds. In Tumanyan, 2,390 of 2,520 participants voted for Civil Contract (95.1%), 123 voted against (4.9%), and seven ballots were invalid, according to Mkrtchyan.
On Sunday, Lermontovo in the Lori province, Ferik in Armavir, and Arzni in Kotayk also held local elections. In Lermontovo, Edik Chakhalyan, backed by Civil Contract, was re-elected community head with 96.6%, Governor Mkrtchyan announced.
In Ferik and Arzni, only the city council was elected. Ferik is a Yezidi-populated village where five people were nominated for five positions. At the time of writing, the Central Electoral Commission had not yet published the official results, but announced the voter turnout figures for Tumanyan (around 60%), Ferik (57%), Lermontovos (35%), and Arzni (45%).

items.title: EU sanctions head of camps ‘indoctrinating’ Ukrainian children in North Caucasus
items.summary: Ali Chomaev runs two centres known for holding children taken from Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories.
items.body_text:
The EU has sanctioned Ali Chomaev, who heads education centres and camps for children in the North Caucasus, for the ‘deportation and forcible transfer’ of Ukrainian children to Russia for ‘ideological indoctrination and military education’.
Chomaev, the director of the Adel children’s camp in Dombai, Karachay–Cherkessia and the Solnechny Bereg (‘Sunny Beach’) education centre in Daghestan, was among 10 individuals and 17 entities recently sanctioned by the EU.
According to the EU, they are linked to the ‘systematic unlawful deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children to the Russian Federation and within temporarily occupied territories, as well as their forced assimilation, including ideological indoctrination and military education’.
The EU’s justification says that Adel receives children from the occupied territories of Ukraine, and that the camp’s programmes combine recreation with ideological and military-patriotic training. According to the EU, the camp’s educational programmes focus on patriotism, civic loyalty, Russian state historical narratives, and the promotion of military service.
According to Russia’s consumer protection agency, Rospotrebnadzor, Adel was designed to accommodate 130 children aged between seven and 17 in 2026.
The EU also sanctioned the Solnechny Bereg centre in Daghestan for the same reasons.
OC Media found the presence of Ukrainian children confirmed at both camps in Russian official publications.
On 2 June 2025, the Daghestani Ministry of Education and Science said that 92 children from the Mikhailovsky district of the occupied part of Zaporizhzhia region had arrived at the camp. They were accompanied by four adults. According to the ministry, the children were due to spend 21 days at Solnechny Bereg.
On 23 July of the same year, state-run news agency RIA Daghestan reported the arrival of a group of children from Russia’s Kursk region. The publication said that children from the occupied part of Zaporizhzhia region were also staying at Solnechny Bereg at the time. Among other activities, the children from the Kursk region were scheduled to take part in the Zarnitsa 2.0 competition. The game is a revival of the Soviet Zarnitsa competition and has been held since 2024. Veterans of Russia’s full-scale war in Ukraine serve as mentors for the children who participate in military-style activities such as capturing positions, artillery strikes and storming fortified areas.
In May 2026, Karachay–Cherkessia Head Rashid Temrezov said that ‘160 children from the Starobilsk municipal district of the Ukraine’s Russian-occupied Luhansk came to Karachay–Cherkessia for a holiday’. According to him, the children were accommodated at the Adel and Grand Victoria camps. He noted that in total, 750 children from Ukraine’s Russian-occupied Luhansk will arrive in Karachay–Cherkessia in 2026.
In September 2025, the administration of the Ersakon rural settlement also reported that children from Ukraine’s Russian-occupied Luhansk had stayed at Adel.
The EU had previously imposed sanctions on Russian organisations and officials accused of involvement in the unlawful deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children. In May 2026, the EU Council announced restrictions against 16 individuals and seven entities on similar grounds.
The sanctions include a travel ban to EU countries and an asset freeze. EU citizens and companies are also prohibited from providing funds or economic resources to those on the sanctions list.
According to the EU, since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion, Russia has deported or forcibly transferred more than 20,500 Ukrainian children.

items.title: No constitutional barrier to housing company smoking bans, committee finds
items.summary: Housing companies banning smoking are comparable to other rules on nighttime noise, according to the constitutional law committee's chair.
items.body_text:
The Finnish Parliament's Constitutional Law Committee has found that a housing company can decide to ban smoking without constitutional obstacles.
The government has proposed that housing companies could in the future decide to ban smoking on their properties. Currently, a municipality can impose a ban if a housing company wishes.
According to committee chair Heikki Vestman (NCP), banning smoking is comparable to, for example, housing company rules on nighttime noise.
The Constitutional Law Committee published its statement on the matter on Tuesday.

items.title: Double delivery for Turku twins — Sisters give birth on same day in same hospital
items.summary: The same midwife and medical student were also present at both sisters' deliveries at the maternity hospital in Turku.
items.body_text:
Twin sisters have given birth on the same day at the same hospital in Turku.
According to a post on Instagram by the Turku University Hospital's Women's Clinic, the coincidences did not end there — as the same midwife and medical student were also present at both sisters' deliveries.
"What are the odds that twin sisters give birth on the same day — and, on top of that, have the same midwife present at both deliveries?"
The Instagram post shows midwife Johanna alongside the two mothers and their newborns.
Although rare, incidents of twin sisters giving birth on the same day at the same hospital are not unheard of.
Texas twins Rachel Schmidtberger and Lindsey Denny did just that last year, according to a report by US network ABC News, while in Australia identical twins Nicole and Renee Baillee gave birth just minutes apart on the same maternity ward in Queensland in 2024.

items.title: Survey: Pension pessimism grows among Finns — yet few want the system overhauled
items.summary: Cuts to the pension system seem increasingly likely as Finland looks to make some 10 billion euros in fiscal adjustments over the coming years.
items.body_text:
There is an increasing lack of confidence among people in Finland about the pension system's ability to provide for them in retirement.
This trend of growing uncertainty is clear from the results of a survey conducted by the Finnish Pension Alliance TELA.
Some 60 percent of respondents to the survey said they consider it likely that earnings-related pensions will no longer cover living costs by the year 2050.
People under the age of 59 were especially pessimistic about the future scenario, with up to 72 percent of respondents in some age groups expressing doubts about the pension system's sustainability.
"I think that especially among younger generations, the answers also reflect a lot of general uncertainty about their own future overall," Tela CEO Saara-Sofia Sirén said.
This thinking has likely been influenced by recent public debates about pensions, in which it has been suggested that the burden of paying for proposed reforms will likely fall on younger generations, Sirén further noted.
A survey published by the Finnish Centre for Pensions earlier this year also found that an increasing number of young adults in Finland are saving money for retirement, partly due to concerns about whether the pension system will provide a sufficient income in the future.
Slow change preferred over immediate overhaul
However, despite the growing concerns, TELA's survey also found that a majority of Finns still trust the current pension system model, and few seem willing to change it.
More than three-in-four respondents thought that earnings-related pensions should remain a mandatory system.
Respondents were also fairly unanimous that pension funds should not be used for other purposes, with just 11 percent expressing the view that funds in the earnings-related pension system should be used for purposes other than paying pensions.
Sirén said she interprets the responses as meaning that people are not looking for a major, immediate overhaul of the pension system — but rather a gradual, long-term development over the coming decades.
"Finns want the promise of the current system to hold in the future too, and for it to be something they can rely on," she said.
TELA's survey was carried out by pollster Verian, with research data gathered via an online survey between 14 and 21 August 2026. A total of 1,019 respondents contributed to the survey, with the results weighted to be representative of each target demographic. The margin of error is a maximum 3.1 percentage points in either direction.
Pension cuts increasingly likely
The Finnish state needs to make some 10 billion euros in fiscal adjustments over the coming years, as the country grapples with a spiralling general government deficit and high unemployment rate.
Writing in Työeläke magazine, Mika Niemelä of the Finance Ministry said such a figure cannot be achieved without touching pensions.
"Pension expenditure makes up about a quarter of all public spending. It's hard to see it being completely bypassed in this discussion," Niemelä wrote.
He suggested that possible measures could include extending working careers, cutting pension indices, or tightening pension taxation.
The Finance Ministry is currently drafting various options with a view to publishing them later in the autumn.
The issue is a hot political topic, especially in the run-up to next year's parliamentary elections, with Finance Minister Riikka Purra (Finns) stating last year that the government had sought to make fiscal adjustments without touching pensions.

items.title: 'Disturbing' waiting times irrelevant in key Swedish citizenship ruling
items.summary: This week’s Sweden in Focus Extra features an interview with Fredrik Löndahl, Chief Judge at the Migration Court in Malmö.
items.body_text:
Not yet a member of The Local? Join now with this special offer for podcast listeners.
Sweden's government tightened rules for citizenship earlier this year without transitional rules for people who had already applied. The new rules require eight years of residency instead of five for most applicants, and would-be citizens must now pass language and civics tests.
The Migration Court in Malmö looked very closely recently at a case in which an applicant appealed for their right to be awarded citizenship according to the old rules. But the court ruled against the citizenship applicant in a blow to people who had waited in the queue and were hoping to become Swedish citizens under the rules that were in place at the time of application.
Some hope was restored however when the judge told The Local's Richard Orange that an appeal to a higher court could succeed.
In this week's episode you can hear an excerpt from the interview with Judge Löndahl we well as a studio discussion about the case and what happens next.
Host James Savage is joined this week by panelists Emma Löfgren and Richard Orange.

items.title: Sweden's Green Party calls for immediate stop to teen deportations
items.summary: Sweden's Green Party have tabled a motion in parliament calling for an immediate and permanent stop to teen deportations, arguing that those affected do not have time to wait for government talks to be completed.
items.body_text:
In a motion submitted to the parliament on Monday, the party called for four different measures which will stop deportations, make it easier for those who have already been deported to return to Sweden, and make it easier for those applying for a study permit to afford their tuition.
"We don't know how long it is going to take to form a government, but the young people don't have any more time to wait," Annika Hirvonen, the Green Party's group leader in the parliament, told the Aftonbladet newspaper.
It remains uncertain which parties will even be in the eventual government, she conceded. "But a parliamentary majority has said that they want to stop this for real. That's why we are tabling this proposal now."
The motion is a so-called "independent" motion or fristående motion, which MPs can submit in the Swedish parliament every autumn between parliament's opening and the deadline for submitting the budget, which this year falls on November 27th.
The motion will need to be debated and amended in the parliament's Social Insurance Committee, on which the four former opposition parties now have a majority of MPs, before being submitted to the parliament.
Hirvonen told Aftonbladet that she had already received a commitment from the Centre Party and Left Party to support the motion and said it remained to be seen whether the Social Democrats would also support it.
In the motion, the party goes beyond calling for parliament to vote for the government to institute a permanent bar on the deportations of teenagers and young adults.
It also calls for the government to bring back the "particularly distressing circumstances" safety clause; to change the Aliens Act so that young adults who have already been deported can return to Sweden; and to change university funding rules so that young people who have grown up in Sweden have the same right to free higher education as Swedish citizens.
Sweden's Migration Minister Johan Forssell was critical of the motion, saying it went well beyond what was necessary to end teen deportations, and arguing that it seemed designed to put pressure on the Social Democrats.
"Since the Social Democrats voted to remove the provision allowing for 'particularly distressing circumstances', this should probably instead be seen as an intervention in their negotiations," he wrote in a text message.
He added that the Tidö government's solution to the deportation of teenagers – which will allow young people to receive permits as dependants of their parents up until the age of 21 – comes into force this Thursday, October 1st.
"The government's solution will therefore be in place long before the Green Party's motion can be considered by parliament," he said.

items.title: Six keys to understanding autumn in Sweden
items.summary: The summer is drawing to a close. With that in mind, now is a good time to roll out some common Swedish autumn topics and phrases to help you navigate your way through the darker days.
items.body_text:
1. Winter is coming
It feels cruel to start an article on autumn with the subject of winter, but there's no escaping the fact that they days are getting shorter this time of the year.
The official arrival of vintertid (winter time) comes on October 25th in 2026, meaning the clocks move back an hour – and by extension, you get to lie an hour longer in bed that day without feeling guilty.
2. Clothes, weather, and the most annoying Swedish phrase ever
The changing of the seasons means more rain, and in turn that means an increased chance of encountering perhaps the most irritating Swedish phrase of all time.
Ever had the audacity to suggest it's not much fun spending time outdoors in the pouring rain? You may well have been met by the response det finns inget dåligt väder, bara dåliga kläder, meaning "there's no such thing as bad weather, only bad clothing".
Apart from being fundamentally false (tell someone caught in a hurricane that all they need is a better jacket, then get back to me), it's the glee with which this one is wheeled out that's particularly annoying. But you may as well know what it means, as it's guaranteed to happen.
3. Cosiness, cosiness everywhere
Bad weather isn’t all bad, admittedly. The cold autumn air also means höstmys – roughly translated, autumn cosiness, which most visibly manifests itself in the reappearance of candles, cups of hot chocolate (or tea, or coffee depending on your preference), a greater inclination towards baked goods, the return of your favourite warm jumper, and if you're feeling particularly creative, a chance to use some of the brightly coloured leaves that are now in abundance to decorate your home.
Look out for interior sites and magazines sharing their höstmystips – a dead cert at this time of the year.
4. Much ado about mushrooms
Autumn means it's prime svampplockning (mushroom picking) season in Sweden, the biggest thing since blåbärsplockning (blueberry picking) season, or whatever other season it happened to be before that.
The point is, Swedes like to make use of their natural resources, and at this time of the year a favourite weekend hobby is to find your nearest forest and go mushroom hunting.
Beware of poisonous mushrooms, but do keep an eye out for key types like trattkantareller (yellowfoot) and smörsopp (sticky bun), while there may also be a few stensoppar (penny buns) left over from the summer.
Oh, and accept that your Swedish friends are probably bigger experts than you (they have mushroom smarts in this part of the world, don't you know) and learn from them!
5. The apple of Sweden's eye
Mushrooms aren’t the only food that thrives in the cold conditions: The apples are ripe for harvest in the south of Sweden, and that means it's time for äppelmust (cloudy apple juice) äppelpaj (apple pie) and äppelmos (apple sauce). Oh, and it doesn’t hurt to try some äppelcider (apple cider), for good measure.
You likely won't miss the fact that this fruit is in abundance in the autumn: Swedish supermarkets tend to give them pride of place while they're in season.
6. Britt and her late summer
To end on an optimistic point, if there are a few unusually warm days in the middle of autumn, the chances are you'll hear Swedes talking about a Brittsommar.
That’s the term used here for a period of late, unseasonably pleasant weather that us English speakers tend to refer to as an Indian summer. The Swedish name comes from the October 7th name day for Birgitta and Britta – fingers crossed we get to use it this year!
Article written by Lee Roden in 2017
items.normalised_title: six keys to understanding autumn in sweden

items.title: What's on in Germany: 10 unmissable events in October 2026
items.summary: From giant pumpkin displays and harvest traditions to illuminated landmarks and Halloween scares, October is one of the most varied months of the year for events in Germany.
items.body_text:
October is when Germany begins to change pace. Beer gardens start to empty, mornings become noticeably cooler and forests take on shades of gold and copper as autumn settles across the country.
It's also one of the year's most distinctive months for festivals and cultural events. Alongside harvest celebrations and wine festivals, you'll find some of Germany's biggest literary, artistic and historical events, as well as plenty of traditions that international visitors may never have encountered before.
Whether you're looking for onion markets, pumpkin sculptures, illuminated cityscapes or a castle full of Halloween monsters, here are 10 events worth seeking out across Germany this October.
October 2nd to 4th: German Unity Day celebrations, Bremen
Germany's national holiday falls on October 3rd each year, marking the reunification of East and West Germany in 1990. Unfortunately for workers hoping for an extra day off, the holiday lands on a Saturday in 2026, but that doesn't stop the celebrations.
Each year the official national festivities move to a different federal state. In 2026, Bremen takes on hosting duties, transforming its city centre and waterfront into a huge open-air festival stretching from the historic centre to the banks of the Weser.
Much of the programme is free and outdoors. Visitors can wander between stages hosting concerts, theatre performances, debates, readings and family activities, while all 16 German states showcase their cultures on the popular Ländermeile.
Big-name acts including Die Fantastischen Vier, MiA., ClockClock and Kamrad are scheduled to appear across the weekend, while a special evening production along the river promises one of the event's visual highlights.
READ ALSO: How October 3rd became German Unity Day
October 7th to 11th: Frankfurt Book Fair, Frankfurt
The Frankfurt Book Fair is one of the most important publishing and media events in the world, bringing together everyone from global publishers and bestselling authors to comic artists and devoted readers.
While the first days are geared towards the publishing industry, the public programme opens up from Friday onwards. This year's guest of honour is Czechia, while the fair is also placing a particular emphasis on fan communities and popular genres, including romance, fantasy, crime fiction, manga and children's literature.
Cosplay has become one of the defining features of the event, with dedicated contests and performances taking place throughout the weekend.
Elsewhere, visitors can browse the huge comics and manga areas, attend author signings, meet literary stars, explore Japanese and Korean pop culture showcases or simply spend the day people-watching.
READ ALSO: The six novels battling to win the German Book Prize 2026
October 9th to 11th: Weimar Onion Market, Weimar
Few German festivals are as delightfully niche as the Weimar Onion Market. Dating back to 1653, it’s the oldest folk festival in Thuringia and has grown into one of the country's most distinctive autumn celebrations.
For one weekend each October, Weimar's historic centre fills with hundreds of traders selling intricately braided onion wreaths known as Zwiebelzöpfe. There are also stalls serving onion tart, regional specialities, local wine and beer, while multiple stages host live music and entertainment across the city.
This year's event will also see newly crowned Onion Queen Roswitha I officially open proceedings with the traditional cutting of the onion tart.
October 9th to 18th: Festival of Lights, Berlin
Berlin has no shortage of landmarks, and for 10 nights in October many become works of art in their own right.
During the Festival of Lights, major sights across the capital are transformed by large-scale projections, illuminations and video installations. The Brandenburg Gate, Berlin Cathedral and the Fernsehturm are typically among the best-known locations, though dozens of buildings participate each year.
