items.title: Shein shares dive more than 11% after earnings disappoint
items.summary: Shares in Chinese fast-fashion giant Shein plunged more than 11 percent in Hong Kong on Tuesday after releasing disappointing financial results. The company has faced scrutiny over its environmental footprint and allegations of human rights violations, and faces growing competition from low-cost e-commerce companies such as Temu and AliExpress. The firm said on Monday that […]
items.body_text:
Shares in Chinese fast-fashion giant Shein plunged more than 11 percent in Hong Kong on Tuesday after releasing disappointing financial results.
The company has faced scrutiny over its environmental footprint and allegations of human rights violations, and faces growing competition from low-cost e-commerce companies such as Temu and AliExpress.
The firm said on Monday that revenue grew just one percent on-year in the first six months of the year, while its operating profit halved.
By around lunch on Tuesday, Shein’s share price had pared some of the losses but was still down 10.9 percent at HK$31.44.
Monday’s results were Shein’s first since its high-profile initial public offering this month, which put the company’s valuation at around $26.3 billion — well short of the nearly $100 billion during private fundraising rounds in 2022.
Net revenue from Europe fell 13.9 percent to nearly $3.8 billion for the second quarter, Shein reported.
The decrease “reflects a decline in sales volume as we raised prices and lowered online advertising spending” in anticipation of the removal of the customs duty exemption, the company said.
Another key market, the United States, saw revenue drop six percent in April-June, reflecting the impact of tariffs.
Since its first day of trading on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange in September, Shein’s share price has fallen more than 35 percent.
The accelerating decline in Shein’s operating profit “clouds the extent of a 2027 recovery from freight relief and an unproven push into higher-priced brands”, said Catherine Lim, an analyst at Business Intelligence.
“Management plans to absorb freight and tariff costs rather than raise prices to protect the company’s competitive position,” she said, adding that localising stock in Europe will lead to higher logistics costs in the short term.

items.title: Hong Kong authorities hail scheme for reducing sodium levels in bread by average of up to 17%
items.summary: Hong Kong authorities have hailed a health scheme that encouraged bread manufacturers to cut sodium levels by an average of up to 17 per cent, following a report that found most adults in the city consume more salt than the recommended daily intake. The Centre for Food Safety (CFS) said on Tuesday that, since the […]
items.body_text:
Hong Kong authorities have hailed a health scheme that encouraged bread manufacturers to cut sodium levels by an average of up to 17 per cent, following a report that found most adults in the city consume more salt than the recommended daily intake.
The Centre for Food Safety (CFS) said on Tuesday that, since the scheme was rolled out in 2019, all participating bread manufacturers have met the voluntary sodium reduction targets for their white and wholemeal bread products.
They include seven manufacturers of pre-packaged bread and 19 manufacturers of non-packaged bread, which together produce about 80 types of white and wholemeal bread products, according to the CFS, an agency under the Food and Environmental Department.
Under the scheme, manufacturers are encouraged to keep the level of sodium in white bread at below 380 milligrams for every 100 grams of white bread, with a cap of 490 milligrams.
For every 100 grams of wholemeal bread, the average sodium level should not exceed 380 milligrams. The maximum level is 470 milligrams, according to the guidelines.
“After the implementation of the Scheme, the average sodium content of related bread products decreased by 10 per cent to 17 per cent, with some manufacturers successfully reducing the sodium content of their products by more than 40 per cent,” a spokesperson for the CFS said in the statement on Tuesday, which is World Heart Day.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended that an adult should not exceed five grams of salt intake per day, equivalent to 2000 milligrams of sodium.
According to a survey conducted by the Department of Health between 2020 and 2022, Hongkongers aged 15 to 84 had a daily salt intake of 8.4 grams.
The survey also found that more than 80 per cent of Hongkongers aged 15 to 84 had a salt intake above the WHO recommended daily limit.
High salt intake increases the risk of cardiovascular disease and stroke by raising blood pressure.
“As we observe World Heart Day, the CFS reminds the public of the importance of reducing sodium intake in lowering the risk of high blood pressure, thereby promoting heart health and preventing cardiovascular diseases,” the government agency said.
It added that it had provided training and testing for bread manufacturers to reformulate their products to reduce sodium levels.

items.title: Hong Kong man charged with voyeurism over hiding pinhole cameras in gym
items.summary: A Hong Kong man has been charged with voyeurism after he was arrested for allegedly installing hidden pinhole cameras in a gym changing room. Fung Kwok-wang, a 34-year-old worksite foreman, left the Shatin Magistrates’ Courts on Tuesday morning after being granted bail. He was arrested on Sunday, after videos of a pinhole camera taped to […]
items.body_text:
A Hong Kong man has been charged with voyeurism after he was arrested for allegedly installing hidden pinhole cameras in a gym changing room.
Fung Kwok-wang, a 34-year-old worksite foreman, left the Shatin Magistrates’ Courts on Tuesday morning after being granted bail.
He was arrested on Sunday, after videos of a pinhole camera taped to a removable ceiling panel circulated on social media.
The camera was discovered by a staff member at a 24/7 Fitness branch in Sha Tin, police said.
According to a court document, Fung was charged with one count of voyeurism, alleging that he installed or operated a pinhole camera at the Sha Tin gym between September 24 and 25 to enable himself or any other person to commit a voyeurism offence under the city’s Crimes Ordinance.
The gym chain has suspended Fung’s membership and stepped up checks across all branches.
Storage devices seized
Police said in a Monday press conference that three pinhole cameras were found in the changing rooms at the gym on Lek Yuen Street.
Sha Tin District chief inspector Ng Yuk-pui said that the cameras were seized along with three memory cards found in three separate individual changing rooms at the gym.
The gym has two female toilets, one male toilet, and four unisex individual changing rooms, each with a shower area and changing space, Ng said.
Police identified the suspect after conducting digital forensic analysis of footage stored on the cards. Ng said the police were not able to reveal how many videos were stored on the cards as the case had entered legal proceedings.
Officers also seized hard drives and other devices from Fung’s residence.
Asked whether the police would take action against sellers of the pinhole cameras, Ng said that the suspect bought the cameras on a well-known mainland Chinese e-commerce platform, which would pose limitations on enforcement.
According to local media reports, Fung was believed to have bought the cameras from Taobao.

China’s generative AI user base crosses 700 million, covering over half the population
Nearly half of users employ AI tools to process images or videos, while 38 per cent use it for text processing and 33 per cent for work notes
China’s generative artificial intelligence user base surpassed 700 million at the end of June, accounting for more than half of the population as wide AI adoption pushes the technology’s penetration rate to a record high in the country.
The user base data, released Tuesday by the China Internet Network Information Centre, represents an increase of 16 per cent from the end of 2025, when China had 602 million generative AI users with a penetration rate of 42.8 per cent.
Question-and-answer services remain the most common use of generative AI in China. In a survey of users, 76 per cent said they used the technology to seek answers. Nearly half, or 48 per cent, employed AI tools to process images or videos, while 38 per cent used it for text processing and 33 per cent for work summaries, meeting notes or presentations.
The report said AI adoption had also expanded beyond software. Some 39 per cent of users had bought smart hardware online during the past six months.

Hong Kong police record 1,503 suspicious iPhone charges so far worth HK$30m
Police say all unauthorised iPhone 18 Pro transactions have been cancelled and Apple has been asked to review its payment security measures
Hong Kong police have received more than 1,500 reports of suspicious credit card transactions involving Apple’s new iPhone 18 Pro series, totalling more than HK$30 million (US$3.82 million).
In an update on the case, which has drawn public attention, the force said the number of reports had risen to 1,503 as of Tuesday, from about 1,200 two weeks earlier. It added that all the transactions had been cancelled.
Speaking at a Kowloon City district council meeting, Commissioner of Police Joe Chow Yat-ming noted that in the cases involved, Apple’s online commerce security measures were not in effect and the transactions did not require verification.
“This meant that one-time passwords or mobile app verification were not required, allowing fraudsters to place large orders using illegally obtained credit card information,” he said.

items.title: Satellite data shows North Korea’s 2026 crop conditions on par with last year
items.summary: Satellite analysis of North Korea’s crop conditions in August 2026 shows farmland across the country growing at almost exactly the same pace as last year, pointing to a harvest roughly in line with 2025 as the country continues to struggle with chronic food shortages. I analyzed vegetation index data from the Joint Polar Satellite System […]
items.body_text:
Satellite analysis of North Korea’s crop conditions in August 2026 shows farmland across the country growing at almost exactly the same pace as last year, pointing to a harvest roughly in line with 2025 as the country continues to struggle with chronic food shortages.
I analyzed vegetation index data from the Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS), a series of weather satellites operated by the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and NASA, to assess the health of North Korean crops this year. The data, distributed by the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) as eVIIRS NDVI, showed only a marginal rise in the peak August vegetation index on North Korean farmland. This indicates that overall crop vigor has held at about the same level as a year earlier.
The Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) gauges how much healthy green vegetation covers an area by comparing how plants reflect visible and near-infrared light. Values closer to 1.0 indicate denser and more vigorous plant growth, which makes NDVI a standard tool for tracking crops from space.
Favorable weather helped this year, as reservoirs held enough water in the spring and the summer brought plenty of sunlight. However, chronic shortages of farming supplies, combined with an August heat wave and drought that hit dryland crops, kept North Korea from achieving any major gains in productivity.
Taken together, these factors suggest that North Korea’s 2026 harvest will look much like last year’s. The final yield could still shift, however, depending on whether autumn typhoons or floods strike first. In the fall of 2025, typhoons bypassed the Korean Peninsula, and the harvest turned out relatively better than the year before. If the country avoids major typhoon damage again this year, I expect it to maintain a stable harvest on par with last year’s.
Food production remains a pressing issue for the Kim Jong Un regime, which has repeatedly pressed farms to boost grain output.
Mapping crop conditions across 1.9 million hectares
To assess crop conditions in August 2026, I combined a land use map based on the European Space Agency’s Sentinel-2 satellites with eVIIRS imagery. I extracted North Korea’s cultivated land from the 2025 global land use map produced at a 10-meter resolution by ESRI, a U.S. geographic information systems company. That data puts North Korea’s total farmland at about 1.9 million hectares. Overlaying the eVIIRS imagery on this farmland data gave me a framework for tracking how well crops are growing.
I built the vegetation index data using maximum value compositing (MVC), a technique that keeps only the highest readings from a set of images. In this case, I drew on eVIIRS data observed at a 350-meter resolution throughout August 2026. This process filters out interference from clouds and shadows so that the composite reflects only vegetation vigor. Crop vegetation index values generally peak close to 1.0 in mid-August, when growth is most active, and then gradually decline until harvest. For this reason, the August maximum value composite serves as a reliable benchmark for judging the state of the crops.
Using this refined satellite data, I compared vegetation changes against the same period last year. North Korean farmland recorded a vegetation index of 0.867 in August 2026, slightly higher than the 0.863 measured in August 2025. items.title: South Hwanghae grain store managers escape punishment after hiking rice prices
items.summary: Managers of state-run grain stores in North Korea’s South Hwanghae province pushed rice prices well above market rates in September 2026. Provincial authorities summoned them over the price hikes, but the managers returned to work without facing real punishment. The managers run grain stores in four counties of the province: Songhwa, Jaeryong, Unryul and Ryongyon. […]
items.body_text:
Managers of state-run grain stores in North Korea’s South Hwanghae province pushed rice prices well above market rates in September 2026. Provincial authorities summoned them over the price hikes, but the managers returned to work without facing real punishment.
The managers run grain stores in four counties of the province: Songhwa, Jaeryong, Unryul and Ryongyon. They were urgently summoned to the South Hwanghae provincial people’s committee on Sept. 19, a source in the province told Daily NK on Monday.
Under Kim Jong Un, North Korea has expanded its network of state-run grain stores in recent years. The policy aims to pull the rice and corn trade away from private markets and bring food prices back under state control. Donju, meaning “masters of money,” are newly wealthy entrepreneurs who finance much of North Korea’s commercial activity.
The grain stores began selling rice at 56,000 North Korean won per kilogram on Sept. 1. Market rice prices were hovering around 50,000 won per kilogram at the time, so the stores charged over 10% more.
Some stores sold large quantities of rice at that price from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. every day. Within a few days, they had raised the price as high as 60,000 won.
Local people then filed a string of complaints with the provincial party committee, the source said. The managers were eventually called before the provincial people’s committee for questioning.
The managers were held separately at designated locations from Sept. 19 to 20, according to the source. There they attended ideological review sessions and wrote formal statements of self-criticism.
The provincial people’s committee accused the managers of four main violations of state pricing rules. First, they unilaterally raised the price to 56,000 won on Sept. 1. Rice was selling for around 50,000 won in other cities and counties across the province at the time.
Second, they set the price as a so-called “wholesale price” meant for bulk trading between merchants. Because it was not a retail price for ordinary customers, it pushed up rice prices in nearby markets.
The managers were also faulted for opening their stores for 12 hours a day without state approval. They were further criticized for later raising prices to around 60,000 won, which deepened supply instability.
Donju behind rice prices avoid harsh punishment
The harsh punishment that many local people had expected never came, however. “The managers wrote a few pages of self-criticism and went through an ideological review session,” the source said. “Then they went straight back to their stores as if nothing had happened.”
“At first it looked like officials were going to make a big deal of it,” the source added. “In the end, though, nothing much came of the whole case.”
The managers are not simply heads of state institutions but donju who have poured large sums into the stores. They reportedly used personal funds to build the store facilities and set up their own rice supply networks. They even pay the wages of store employees out of their own pockets, according to the source.
In some parts of North Korea, state agencies nominally oversee grain stores while private traders handle the actual business. Donju and merchants are deeply involved in procuring and selling grain behind the state’s official front. Some stores have recently begun raising grain prices ahead of local markets, which then drives up market prices.
The provincial people’s committee and law enforcement agencies reportedly found it hard to take firm action as a result. They feared that punishing or removing the managers could destabilize the local rice supply chain.
The source said the donju‘s long-standing financial ties with provincial officials also shaped how the case was handled.
“People say there isn’t a single provincial official who doesn’t owe these four donju a favor,” the source said. “If they shut down the grain stores, food distribution across every city and county would be in an uproar right away.”

items.title: Poor road conditions leave North Korean drivers paying for constant tire repairs
items.summary: Poor road conditions across North Korea’s North Hamgyong province are driving up tire costs for drivers in 2026. Cracked asphalt, deep potholes and long unpaved stretches are wearing out tires within months of purchase. Many drivers now find themselves stuck in a costly cycle of repairs and replacements that eats into their earnings. Drivers who […]
items.body_text:
Poor road conditions across North Korea’s North Hamgyong province are driving up tire costs for drivers in 2026. Cracked asphalt, deep potholes and long unpaved stretches are wearing out tires within months of purchase. Many drivers now find themselves stuck in a costly cycle of repairs and replacements that eats into their earnings.
Drivers who earn a living with their vehicles in Hoeryong and Chongjin are growing frustrated by constant flat tires. A source in North Hamgyong province shared the complaints with Daily NK on Monday.
“Some drivers have to replace their tires again less than a year after putting on new ones,” the source said. “That’s why there’s so much anger about the state of the roads.”
Some roads in North Korea are paved, but the state rarely maintains them and many surfaces are in bad shape. The asphalt often cracks and potholes open up after the summer monsoon season and the winter freeze.
In most cases, local authorities handle repairs by mobilizing ordinary people and employees of state agencies and enterprises. North Korea routinely drafts citizens into unpaid labor for construction, farming and infrastructure projects. These campaigns often come with demands for cash or materials that work like an informal tax.
“Ordinary people who aren’t experts get mobilized for road repairs, and they have to pay for materials too,” the source said. “They also have to do the actual work themselves, which is a heavy burden on them.”
“Many of them take part only reluctantly, so they cut costs wherever they can,” the source added. “They spend the money they collect sparingly, and the repairs often end up being just for show.”
“Even after the roads are fixed, you can hardly see any difference, and they soon go back to how they were,” he said. “Drivers who keep using these roads pay for repairs and replacements over and over because their tires wear out so easily.”
Poor road conditions eat into drivers’ earnings
One driver in his 40s from North Hamgyong province spent 3,000 Chinese yuan (about $420) on new tires this spring. Even so, he has needed to have punctures patched several times since then, according to the source.
“Maybe it’s because the roads are so bad, but my tires keep getting holes and going flat,” the driver said. “It feels like I’m making money, but it keeps going into repairs for the tires and the rest of the car.”
“With more and more vehicles on the roads in our country, we need a ‘great road revolution’ now,” he said. “Otherwise, drivers like me will just keep getting stuck with the repair bills.”
The damaged roads cause more than inconvenience for travelers, since higher maintenance costs cut directly into what drivers earn. Tire repairs and replacements have become a recurring expense for drivers who carry passengers and goods for a fee. Privately operated vehicles, often registered under state enterprises, form the backbone of North Korea’s informal transport network.
The frequent tire damage has also kept demand for repair services steady inside North Korea, according to the source. As a result, the country continues to import Chinese-made tires along with the materials and parts needed to fix them.
“Rising demand for tires and repairs may mean more income for dealers and mechanics,” the source said. “But it also means drivers have to pay more, and they pass those costs on to their passengers.”
“In the end, the cost of these bad roads lands on everyone who rides in a vehicle,” he said. “People put their money and labor into road repairs, but nothing really improves, and then they pay higher fares too.”
“That’s why people call it pouring water into a bottomless jar,” the source said.

items.title: Crossland to miss NRL GF with four-game ban for Cleary tackle
items.summary: Newcastle Knights hooker Phoenix Crossland is suspended for four games by the NRL judiciary for the tackle that left Penrith's Nathan Cleary with a broken leg.
items.body_text:
Newcastle Knights hooker Phoenix Crossland has been suspended for four games by the NRL judiciary for the tackle that left Penrith's Nathan Cleary with a broken leg.
Crossland pleaded guilty to the dangerous contact charge on Tuesday before fronting the judiciary to learn his fate.
He will now miss this Sunday's NRL grand final.
The ban would also rule him out of New Zealand's three World Cup pool games.
Crossland was sent off for a hip drop tackle on Cleary in the 36th minute of Newcastle's preliminary final win over the Panthers.
Cleary suffered a compound fracture and a dislocated ankle.
Crossland was represented by barrister James McLeod, who made the case for his client to receive a two or three-week ban.
Crossland cited his career record, telling the judiciary he had never before been sent off. He admitted he got the execution of the tackle wrong but insisted "wasn't trying to hurt anyone".
Arguing for a four-game suspension, the NRL said Crossland's tackle failed to exercise a proper duty of care and, while accidental, did not show enough caution towards Cleary.
Crossland told the judiciary was deeply remorseful for Cleary's injury and had reached out to the Panthers star.
"I called him yesterday. It was obviously a tough phone call," Crossland said.
"I reached out to his dad [Panthers coach Ivan Cleary] as well.
"Nathan was great, he said not to worry about and he understood it was an accident.
"He was such a gentlemen, he told me to stop saying sorry.
"He's my favourite player in the game by a mile. He's the best player in the game and I look up to him."
Crossland described the incident and fallout as a low point in his life. In his submissions, McLeod produced abusive Instagram messages that had been directed towards Crossland in the past 48 hours.
"It's killing me, it's been the worst couple of days of my life," Crossland said.
"It's meant to be the best week of my life and it's been far from it."
The verdict sets up a scenario where 19-year-old Knight Diesel Hagan could make his NRL debut in a grand final.
It would be the first time such a debut has taken place in 90 years. Eddie Lockhart was the last to do it in 1936, for Balmain.
Harrison Graham will almost certainly shift to a starting role for Newcastle in the grand final, while other options for the Knights include Thomas Cant and Jermaine McEwen.

items.title: Brazil beat Socceroos in fractious, entertaining clash
items.summary: The Socceroos once again gave Brazil an enormous scare, but the five-time world champions rallied to secure a 4-2 win at a packed Lang Park in Brisbane.
items.body_text:
Socceroos fall to 4-2 Brazil defeat in front of record Brisbane crowd in international friendly
The Socceroos have fallen to a 4-2 defeat against Brazil in front of 52,423 fans at Lang Park in Brisbane.
Fresh from a superb performance in Townsville on Friday night, the Socceroos will once again take plenty from a contest that ebbed and flowed throughout 90 thoroughly engaging minutes.
With Tony Popovic naming an unchanged team for just the second time in his tenure, it seems likely that this XI is the one that will start the Asian Cup in January.
On the basis of what they showed against the number five team in the world, they should serve Australia very well indeed.
Australia fell behind early to a Brazil team that came out the blocks firing, scoring through a superb Vanderson strike in the opening three minutes.
They could have fallen even further behind when Pat Beach pulled off two sensational saves to twice deny Raphinha just a couple of minutes later.
The Socceroos had barely had control of the ball at that stage, the promised response from a badly burned Brazil team in full evidence.
However, the hosts showed superb composure and self-confidence to hit back, gradually regaining control in the midfield and scoring two goals in the space of four minutes to take the lead mid way through the first half.
Alessandro Circati turned home a corner at the back post, a goal initially ruled out for offside before VAR intervened.
Then, Connor Metcalf prompted an explosion of joy from the home fans in the stands by drilling home a magnificent strike just minutes later, taking a touch and hammering a left-footed shot into the top corner from the edge of the area.
The pressure was clearly getting to Brazil, with the normally Imperturbable Carlo Ancelotti screaming into the face of the assistant referee after Tete Yengi was fouled.
The visitors drew level on the stroke of half time, first of two penalties awarded to the visitors converted by skipper Raphinha after another lengthy VAR review when the referee inexplicably failed to give a penalty after Harry Souttar made a rough challenge.
Tempers threatened to boil over in the second half when Endrick and Souttar clashed, Aziz Behich coming in a sparking a small melee in front of the Socceroos bench.
That finally sparked Brazil, who turned the style back on as Bruno Guimarães finished a sumptuous move from the left to give the visitors the lead.
Vinícius Júnior was then fouled in the penalty area and converted to seal the victory in front of the biggest football crowd ever at Lang Park.
"Honestly, they [the Socceroos] press really well," Ancelotti said.
"They are really well organised, they surprised us in this sense.
"They put much more pressure in the front and we had difficulty to build from the back.
"They are a very good team, in my opinion."

items.title: Silver lining for Freo captain after grand final injury nightmare
items.summary: Fremantle gets some badly needed good news in the wake of its AFL grand final disaster, confirming captain Alex Pearce will not need surgery.
items.body_text:
Fremantle have had some badly needed good news in the wake of its AFL grand final disaster, confirming captain Alex Pearce will not need surgery.
The Dockers are confident the key defender will return to training in the pre-season.
As the post-mortem continues following Saturday's devastating loss to Brisbane, Fremantle said Pearce suffered a partially ruptured Achilles tendon, as well as a calf strain.
Pearce was giving chase early in the third quarter of the grand final when he suddenly fell to the ground.
Two trainers helped him from the field, with one of the most shattering images of the loss being Pearce hobbling past the premiership cup on crutches at the post-game presentations.
Brisbane coach Chris Fagan and several of his players offered their best wishes to Pearce soon after the final siren.
Coach Justin Longmuir said losing the Dockers' defensive general cost them, especially during Brisbane's last-gasp comeback.
"Thankfully Alex has not had a complete rupture of his Achilles tendon and he will not require surgery," Fremantle football boss Joe Brierty said on Tuesday in a club statement.
"Scans have revealed a partial tear of his Achilles tendon and also a significant calf strain.
"As it stands, we expect Alex to return to training in pre-season."
Also on Tuesday, chief executive Simon Garlick was the latest key Docker to defend Wharfie Time and dismiss its activation as a factor in their heartbreaking loss.
Lions coach Chris Fagan and several of his players have said since that they had a plan if Wharfie Time was sounded, vowing they would try to use it to their own advantage.
But Garlick followed Longmuir and Brierty in denying Wharfie Time had torpedoed the Dockers.
"We know teams, including ours, have scenario plans for being a few goals down or up with a few minutes to go," Garlick told SEN.
"Brisbane executed that plan exceptionally well on Saturday, clearly. It's clearly a plan they would've had regardless of Wharfie Time."
It remains unclear whether Wharfie Time is now sunk.
"Our fans love Wharfie Time. We've just lost a grand final in the most heartbreaking way," Garlick said.
"We're not about to throw out things that make us who we are.
"We'll work through that."

items.title: Imams’ council condemns Melbourne Islamic preacher’s call to ‘take up arms’ against enemies
items.summary: Independent MP Allegra Spender says the comments reinforce the need for stronger protection against hate speechGet our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcastAustralia’s peak body for imams says it is “deeply concerned” about reports a Melbourne-based Islamic preacher called for followers to “take up arms against his enemies” and not take “Jews and the Christians for friends”.The Australian National Imams’ Council (ANIC) released a statement on Tuesday after Nine newspapers revealed
items.body_text:
Australia’s peak body for imams says it is “deeply concerned” about reports a Melbourne-based Islamic preacher called for followers to “take up arms against his enemies” and not take “Jews and the Christians for friends”.
The Australian National Imams’ Council (ANIC) released a statement on Tuesday after Nine newspapers revealed the preacher who goes by the name Abu Ahmad made the comments during a sermon in July.
Reading from a book chapter, Ahmad said Muslims should not “take the Jews and the Christians for friends” in a video posted to the social media feed of Melbourne-based Al Bayyinah Islamic Centre in July.
“For the sake of Allah, it includes the obligation to declare enmity for his sake, opposition for the sake of Allah. It is to declare opposition, indeed, to take up arms against his enemies, to shun them, and to stay far from them both in word and deed. This proves that simple opposition of the spirit is not enough and that it must be complete by honouring of your commitment,” he said.
“If the aim of the enemies of Islam, whether they are atheists, or Jews, or Christians, or modernists, or Zionists, or communists, is the emasculation of … the Muslims and the erosion of their unique character in order to make them the ass of the chosen people, as it is put in the protocols of the elders of Zion, then the urgency of this issue should become clear to every Muslim,” he said.
In an Instagram post on Monday, the Al Bayyinah Islamic Centre included a statement from the preacher.
“The statements the article is attributing to me were from a passage of a book that I was reading during a lesson on al-Walāʾ wal-Barāʾ. They were not a personal call from me for Muslims to attack Christians, Jews or other non-Muslims,” the post signed off by Ahmad said.
The post attached a video which he said was an “explanation of that very passage from the same lesson” and explained it “does not permit harming, oppressing or being unjust towards peaceful non-Muslims.
“Unfortunately, quoting the book without including the explanation that followed gives a completely different impression of what was being taught,” the post said.
ANIC said it “strongly and unequivocally condemns any call by any religious or non-religious preacher, leader or individual to take up arms against civilians, religious communities or the Australian people”.
ANIC said it would not make findings about the “individual or the precise context of the reported remarks” until it could properly review material.
ANIC reiterated it “categorically rejects incitement to violence, hatred or harm against any person or community”.
“The safety, security and wellbeing of Australia and the Australian people are fundamental responsibilities that Australian Muslims, Imams and religious leaders must uphold. Islamic teachings require Muslims to honour the sanctity of human life, fulfil their responsibilities to society and contribute positively to the communities and country in which they live.”
The peak body called on all religious leaders, regardless of faith, to exercise responsibility in their public statements. It added that the alleged conduct of an individual should not be used to condemn or blame an entire faith or community.
The Albanese government was forced to abandon anti-vilification laws that would have given authorities greater powers to crack down on religious leaders who promote hatred on the basis of religions, race, gender or sexuality after it failed to gain support from the Nationals and the Greens.
On Tuesday, the independent federal MP Allegra Spender told Nine newspapers the comments showed “why we needed stronger and nationally consistent hate speech legislation”.

items.title: Revealed: the five-paragraph email OpenAI used to inform Australia about agent attack
items.summary: Executive to front parliamentary committee on AI as ministers reveal how brief message telling them about hack was signed off ‘best’Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcastOpenAI has apologised to Australians for its agent attack on Medicare, and will front parliament next week as the tech company revealed more details about its June hack of Australian government websites.Ministers on Tuesday evening released a brief, five
items.body_text:
OpenAI has apologised to Australians for its agent attack on Medicare, and will front parliament next week as the tech company revealed more details about its June hack of Australian government websites.
Ministers on Tuesday evening released a brief, five paragraph email which OpenAI used to inform the Australian government about the attack. The email was sent to a public inbox monitored by Services Australia on 10 September – nearly three months after the AI agent accessed the website on 18 June – and was signed off with the closing “best”.
The Labor government has publicly voiced its fury at the manner in which OpenAI disclosed the incident. The email itself, obtained by Guardian Australia, advised Services Australia that “an OpenAI model identified a way to make the server carry out instructions sent through the public reporting interface, without a private account or password”.
In a blog post released on Tuesday morning (Aest), OpenAI said it should have handled its response better.
“We also should have handled our response better. We are sorry and working to do better in the future.”
The company also provided more detail on the incident revealed by the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, last week.
OpenAI said it became aware of agent activity on Australian government websites in mid-August after the company reviewed earlier training incidents after the Hugging Face attack in July.
The agents gained non-public access to a Services Australia portal for Medicare statistics, and OpenAI said the agent was able to run commands, retrieve internal files, credentials, and write files, but no patient or client records were accessed.
OpenAI’s email to Services Australia pointed the government to the “affected URL”, a Medicare statistics page on the human services website, as well as specifying an “affected report” – a CSV file, commonly used for spreadsheets.
“We recommend that the team responsible for the service investigate the vulnerability and assess the changes needed to prevent it. We would be glad to brief your security team and provide supporting evidence as available,” OpenAI wrote.
“Best, OpenAl Security Team”.
OpenAI was contacted for comment.
The NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research’s public crime mapping tool was also accessed, with application configuration, operational jobs and logs and website metadata provided to the agency.
The agent discovered an exposed access key to query the Victorian agency for health information’s reporting system to access aggregate survey statistics.
For the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, OpenAI agents retrieved aggregate statistics, but separate attempts to bypass access controls were unsuccessful and the information obtained was publicly available.
Services Australia and the Victorian health department were informed on 10 September, while the NSW bureau of crime stastistics was informed on 18 September.
The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare was not informed until 24 September, as OpenAI deemed it did not meet disclosure thresholds.
“Since then we’ve worked closely with Australian government agencies to share what we’ve learned to date,” OpenAI said. “If we identify any additional affected agencies, we will notify them promptly and directly with the information available and provide updates as further facts emerge.”
The incident occurred after one model was tasked to research government spending per person on medicines for skin conditions in Victoria. The model had difficulty obtaining that information, and OpenAI said “it took actions that we had not authorised it to take” including accessing Services Australia’s Medicare statistics reporting service.
OpenAI said it would commit resources and expertise to affected agencies, and provide Australian government agencies with support to build cyberdefences on critical infrastructure.
Australian government agencies and industries will also be given credits out of OpenAI’s US$1bn (AU$1.4bn) Daybreak fund, w

items.title: Sydney teen taken to hospital after falling from moving bus on northern beaches
items.summary: Transport for NSW, bus operator and Rail, Tram and Bus union investigate after incident on Monday eveningGet our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcastInvestigations are under way after a teenage girl fell from a moving double-decker bus on to a busy road in Sydney’s northern beaches.Emergency services were called to Manly Road at Seaforth on Monday evening after the teenager fell from the B-Line bus near the Spit Bridge. Continue reading...
items.body_text:
Investigations are under way after a teenage girl fell from a moving double-decker bus on to a busy road in Sydney’s northern beaches.
Emergency services were called to Manly Road at Seaforth on Monday evening after the teenager fell from the B-Line bus near the Spit Bridge.
She was treated at the scene for head and hip injuries and taken to Royal North Shore hospital, where a spokesperson confirmed on Tuesday she remained in a stable condition.
A Transport for NSW spokesperson said it was aware of the incident on Spit Road and that the bus had been withdrawn from service while an investigation by bus operator Keolis Northern Beaches and the department takes place.
“The passenger was treated at the scene and taken to hospital with minor injuries,” they said. “We wish the passenger all the best in her recovery.”
The incident has also been reported to the Office of Transport Safety Investigations.
On Tuesday, the Rail, Tram and Bus Union (RTBU) said Keolis Northern Beaches, “must urgently explain how a door on one of its B-Line buses reportedly failed” and that it was investigating reports from drivers that doors on the fleet had opened unexpectedly in the past.
RTBU NSW Tram and Bus Division secretary Peter Grech said private operator Keolis and Transport for NSW must “come clean” about whether warnings had been ignored.
“A 16-year-old girl fell out of a moving bus … onto one of the Northern Beaches’ busiest roads. It is horrifying to think how much worse this could have been,” Grech said. “She should have been safe on that bus and this was undoubtedly a highly traumatic experience for her.
“Drivers are telling us this may not be the first time one of these doors has opened unexpectedly. We are currently checking the circumstances, but Keolis cannot leave passengers wondering whether there were warnings it simply failed to act on.
“If a door can open while a bus is moving, then that bus cannot be carrying the public,” he said.
Keolis responded to Guardian Australia’s request for comment on Tuesday afternoon with a statement confirming it was “aware of an incident that occurred last night on our B-Line service which resulted in a passenger falling from the bus near the Spit Bridge at Seaforth”.
“Our immediate thoughts are with the passenger and her family and wishing for a swift recovery.”
It is understood Bustech double-decker B-Line buses have been taken out of service, although Keolis and Transport for NSW have not confirmed which vehicles were withdrawn or when.
It has not been established when and how earlier concerns were reported to Keolis management, the response drivers received or what steps were taken to control the risk.
It is understood the union is seeking records from Keolis and Transport for NSW under the work health and safety act as part of its investigation.

items.title: ShinyHunters hackers say they won't leak sensitive FBI data
items.summary: The hacking group behind a massive FBI data breach says it will not publish the information it obtained, but it cannot guarantee what will happen with the data it already shared with journalists.
items.body_text:
ShinyHunters hackers say they won't leak sensitive FBI data
A representative added, however, that data they already shared is 'out of our control'
The hacking group behind a massive FBI data breach says it will not publish the information it obtained, but cannot guarantee what will happen with the data it already shared.
ShinyHunters claimed responsibility for stealing a massive trove of data from the FBI last Tuesday — including officials' job assignments, addresses and social security numbers — and gave the law enforcement agency one week to rescind an unflattering statement about the group.
With the deadline approaching, a ShinyHunters representative sent CBC News a statement Monday saying they were never planning to release the sensitive data, adding that the media and the public have "made many false assumptions and wild speculations."
The group has been linked to dozens of cyberattacks targeting large companies and institutions. ShinyHunters typically demand ransom payments in exchange for not releasing sensitive data, but they have been adamant that was not their intention in this case.
Campaign to 'combat disinformation'
ShinyHunters denied asking the FBI for a ransom, but acknowledged "past operations" could leave them open to misinterpretation.
"The reason why we have stated multiple times that this is not extortion is because since the very beginning we had made our decision that we would never publish this data. We have never intended to nor have we ever planned to," the statement said in part.
The group told CBC News that their actions against the FBI were part of a campaign to "combat disinformation" about their tactics.
"If we made this statement normally then this much attention to our words and intentions would've never been this widespread. We'd have been ignored and disregarded. However, now everyone knows what the issue is and what we are doing."
ShinyHunters took issue with an FBI report from May that said, among other things, the group is known to threaten family members of its targets and threaten to release embarrassing or compromising images of its victims.

ShinyHunters denied ever using those tactics and released a statement following last Tuesday's data breach giving the FBI one week to remove or "correct" the report.
The group shared a 5,000-line spreadsheet of breached FBI data with some journalists, which it said represented only a small piece of its claimed two- to three-terabyte trove.
The sample included names, addresses, telephone numbers, dates of birth, social security numbers and emergency contact details for what it claimed were thousands of FBI employees.
When CBC News asked ShinyHunters on Monday whether they have taken any steps to ensure the shared data isn't leaked by other sources, the representative said they "cannot guarantee" what will happen to those samples, "because that is out of our control and certain journalists violated our trust."
'Can't trust them,' researcher says
Ian Lin, an ethical hacker and head of research and development at Toronto-based cybersecurity company Packetlabs, says that's concerning.
He says he's seen "a number of researchers" claiming online to have obtained the data, in addition to journalists.
"There's going to be people that are willing to pay a high price for this data," Lin told CBC News.

items.title: Estonia blames Russia for arson at defence factory that produces vehicles Ukraine has used
items.summary: Estonian authorities said Tuesday they have concluded that an arson attack in mid-August on a defence company that provides military vehicles to Ukraine was an act of sabotage commissioned by Russian security services.
items.body_text:
Estonia blames Russia for arson at defence factory that produces vehicles Ukraine has used
3 Latvian citizens were arrested for mid-August crime and extradited to Estonia
Estonian authorities said Tuesday they have concluded that an arson attack in mid-August on a defence company that provides military vehicles to Ukraine was an act of sabotage commissioned by Russian security services.
Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said that "such actions are absolutely unacceptable" and that Russia's charge d'affaires in Tallinn was being summoned to his ministry.
A fire broke out overnight on Aug. 15 at a building in the Estonian capital used by Milrem Robotics, but was quickly brought under control, the BNS news agency reported. On Aug. 17, two Latvian suspects were detained in neighbouring Latvia, and a third followed the next day.
The suspects were handed over to Estonia.
Milrem has supplied THeMIS unmanned ground vehicles to Ukraine.
The Estonian Internal Security Service said that it has concluded that the arson attack "was a deliberate and pre-planned act commissioned by Russian security services."
It said in a statement that "the modus operandi of the Milrem attack is consistent with other acts of sabotage carried out in Europe on behalf of Russia," adding that it "assesses that the attack is directly attributable to the Russian Federation."
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal wrote on X that "we will not be intimidated."
Russia scoffs at accusation
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that "such statements are unfounded, ill-considered, absolutely not reflecting the reality, not containing any substantiation whatsoever."
"We cannot take such statements seriously, and we won't," Peskov said.
Moscow has been widely accused by Western officials of running a campaign of sabotage and disruption with the aim of undermining support for Ukraine and destabilizing European nations.
The Associated Press has tracked around 200 incidents of sabotage and malign activity across Europe blamed on Russia since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022.
That includes organizing plots to set fire to warehouses, launching drones and trying to kill enemies abroad as well as stealing defense technology and carrying out cyberattacks on critical European infrastructure.
In a recent case that pointed to an escalation of such activity, Germany blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August using a drone laden with explosives.

Referencing both the Estonian allegation and the German incident, French President Emmanuel Macron said on social media that Russia "must know that it will not prevail over either our unity or our determination to continue supporting Ukraine."
"The proliferation of these hostile acts reflects a dangerous escalation on the part of Russia, which will only lead it into a dead end," Macron said.
The French leader expressed "full solidarity" with Estonia.
With files from CBC News

Charles Spencer says his new book about his sister, the late Princess Diana, is not an attempt to get revenge on his former in-laws, the British Royal family.
"It's not about settling scores," Spencer, a historian, journalist and the 9th Earl Spencer, told CBC Radio's The Current.
"I could have written something much more devastating," he said. "This was the considered version that I thought, 'Yeah, whatever's in here, needs to be in, to give the full story of Diana's life."
The book, Swan Song: Diana, my sister, has prompted a barrage of international headlines over its claims, including that the then-Prince Charles sounded "giddily elated" when Diana died.
But Spencer said he wrote it in part because he's been inundated with interview requests ahead of the 30th anniversary of her death next year.
"I began to think, 'Well, if everyone wants to know the truth, I think it's time for that,' " he said.
Spencer sat down with The Current's Matt Galloway to discuss the book, and his sister's legacy.
Charles 'upbeat' in call after Diana's death
Diana was arguably the most famous woman in the world after she married Charles in 1981, and gave birth to two sons, William and Harry. But after a tumultuous marriage, the royal couple separated in 1992, finalizing their divorce in 1996.
After leaving the Royal Family, she became a style icon and philanthropist, leading campaigns to clear landmines and challenge stigma around HIV and AIDS.
But she increasingly strained under the glare of the tabloid media and died in a car crash in Paris in 1997, after a high-speed chase while being pursued by paparazzi.
In the book, Spencer claims that Charles sounded "giddily elated" in a phone call after Diana died. Spencer said he'd already received calls from many people wishing to express their shock and offer their condolences.
"He just sounded completely different to everyone else … sort of buoyant … upbeat," he said.
"It was so jarring, particularly among all the sea of other voices."
Spencer also wrote that he argued with Charles in the days following Diana's death, over palace plans for Princes William and Harry to walk behind their mother's coffin in the funeral cortege. Spencer said he told Charles it would be an ordeal Diana would not have wanted her sons to endure.
"He went nuts and started screaming and shouting," Spencer said. "And then he pulled himself together, I thought — and then, he said, 'We'll forget her soon enough.' "
"I was stunned. And I went, 'I can't believe you just said that,' and hung up on him."
Buckingham Palace responded to the allegations earlier this month.
"While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss," the palace said in a statement.
Spencer described the statement as "classic gaslighting."
"They're trying to say maybe it's grief, maybe it was a long time ago, but they're trying to put a question mark over my reliability. It's a tactic, but I don't think it's worked for them."
Funeral procession was 'exhausting emotionally'
Princes William and Harry did walk behind their mother's coffin, alongside Spencer and other family members — with thousands of people thronged on either side of their route.
In the book, Spencer describes it as walking through a tunnel of grief, where the reactions of the crowd kept shifting.
"We could walk for 100 metres and it would be silent, you could just hear sobs. And then [further on], people wailing, like it's a biblical thing, a sort of wailing and gnashing of teeth," he told Galloway, adding that some people screamed out their love for Diana and for her two sons.

items.title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico ask court to extend block on White House ban until case is resolved
items.summary: Outlets say administration has ‘persisted in unpredictably and inconsistently implementing its ban’ despite a judge’s restraining order
items.body_text:
Three news outlets that President Donald Trump abruptly banished from White House grounds this month asked a federal court to block the action until the case is resolved, saying the administration has “persisted in unpredictably and inconsistently implementing its ban” despite a judge’s restraining order – including selectively keeping CNN from participating in White House pool duties.
“The White House’s words and actions leave little doubt that it will immediately reinstitute a complete ban of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO if allowed the opportunity,” lawyers for CNN, MS NOW and Politico wrote in a filing late Monday.
“Because the ban is an unlawful assault on the most fundamental First Amendment freedoms and will inflict irreparable harm on Plaintiffs and the public if not restrained, this Court should preliminarily enjoin its enforcement pending the resolution of this case,” the filing said.
It was the latest development in the back-and-forth saga of the Trump administration and the news media during the second term of his presidency. It has been a contentious relationship that has raised multiple First Amendment questions, produced sanctions and restrictions on White House and Pentagon reporters and led to several lawsuits that are winding their ways through the federal court system.
A two-week temporary restraining order on Trump’s ban of the three organizations, issued by U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly last week, restored the outlets’ White House access, but expires Oct. 8. The preliminary injunction requested in Monday’s filing would extend the White House access until the case is finally resolved.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists return to White House after judge blocks Trump’s ban
In a statement e-mailed to The Associated Press immediately after the filing, the lead attorney for the three news outlets called the ban “a blatant violation of the First Amendment and due process.”
“The president and his administration have continued to make clear that this ban has only one purpose: to punish reporting he doesn’t like,” said the lawyer, Theodore J. Boutrous Jr.
“That’s retaliation and viewpoint discrimination, pure and simple,” Boutrous said. “With the district court’s temporary restraining order expiring this week, it is critical to ensure that the White House continues to be prevented from implementing this unconstitutional ban on the free press.”
White House still says access is a privilege, not a right
The filing came a day after the Trump administration made clear it was not backing down from its contention that the sudden ban, which began Sept. 19, was justified.
“When it comes to the White House, it is the people’s house,” Attorney-General Todd Blanche said on ABC on Sunday, invoking an argument the administration has made since the beginning. “It is a privilege, and not a right, to be there.”
Monday’s 42-page filing reiterated many of the arguments that the news outlets made in their original lawsuit against Trump and the White House, filed two days after the reporters were banned.
It also added mention of the White House broadcast pool rotation, which has become a battleground in the last few days in the standoff between Trump and the media.
The White House, it said, “has persisted in unpredictably and inconsistently implementing its ban, including by barring CNN from fulfilling its role as designated television network pooler on Sept. 26 – to the detriment of CNN, its fellow pool members and, ultimately, the American public.”
When the ban was implemented, CNN was removed from its duties as part of the broadcast pool, which consists of the five main networks: CNN, ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News. In solidarity, the other networks decided to suspend the pool until CNN was allowed back in.

items.title: Tennessee set to execute a woman for the first time in 200 years
items.summary: Christa Pike was 18 when she killed a classmate in a jealous rage and became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row. She is now 50
items.body_text:
Christa Pike was 18 when she killed a classmate in a jealous rage and became one of the youngest women to be sent to death row. Now 50, she is scheduled to be put to death Wednesday in what would be Tennessee’s first execution of a woman in 200 years.
Pike and her boyfriend were convicted in the 1995 killing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, their classmate at Knoxville Job Corps. Prosecutors said Pike feared Slemmer was a romantic rival and lured her to a secluded area where she and her boyfriend tortured and killed Slemmer. The case got widespread attention because of the brutality of the killing, the ages of the people involved and because a satanic symbol was carved into the victim’s body.
Pike does not deny her guilt, but her attorneys and supporters argue a death sentence is not appropriate for a crime committed at that age by a teen with untreated mental illness after a childhood of brutal sexual abuse and neglect. Slemmer’s mother wants the lethal injection to go forward, saying she has waited decades to see Pike’s sentence carried out.
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee announced Monday that he would not grant clemency. Pike’s attorneys have asked the Supreme Court to stay the execution.
Request for clemency points to Pike’s traumatic past
Pike’s attorneys said she experienced an exceptionally traumatic and abusive childhood.
Assistant Federal Defender Stephen Ferrell said Pike was sexually abused starting from when she was a toddler and that she was raped at ages 11 and 17. He said Pike’s lawyers at the penalty phase of her trial did not present the jury with what he said was critical information about her past or argue that her age should be a consideration.
Pike was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. Pike told police she initially only wanted to fight Slemmer but ended up killing her in a frenzied attack. In her clemency petition, Pike’s attorneys said her untreated mental illness and background made her unable to “put the brakes on.”
“I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime,” Pike said in a statement included in her clemency petition.
Ferrell said more today is known about adolescent brain development and that Pike’s death sentence is an outlier. He noted that Pike’s boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, who was 17 at the time, was sentenced to life with the possibility of parole because of his age. He was denied parole last year. A third teen admitted to being an accessory and received probation.
In the modern death penalty era, Ferrell said, other 18-year-olds who were sentenced to death in Tennessee have since had their sentences reduced.
The Death Penalty Information Center said 275 people nationwide have been executed for crimes they committed at age 18, 19 or 20 in the modern death penalty era, but that death sentences for those in that age group have become increasingly rare.
“If Christa Pike was tried today, I do not believe a jury that knew about the documented sexual abuse and neglect she experienced as a child would sentence her to death,” Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said.
Victim’s mother wants the execution to go forward
Speaking by telephone from Florida, Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, also pointed to her daughter’s age and said Slemmer never got a chance to grow up.
“Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run,” Martinez said.
Martinez said her daughter volunteered with the Special Olympics, loved roller skating and wanted to pursue a career in computers.
“She was easygoing. She was a computer geek to begin with. She and my husband would build and tear apart the computers constantly,” Martinez said. “She trusted everybody, and that was her downfall.”

items.title: U.S. prosecutors reopen alleged Cornell University gang rape case after accuser files lawsuit
items.summary: Victim alleges she was drugged and assaulted by seven members of a fraternity in 2024 and that some of the men involved were allowed to write essays to mitigate their conduct
items.body_text:
U.S. prosecutors reopen alleged Cornell University gang rape case after accuser files lawsuit
Victim alleges she was drugged and assaulted by seven members of a fraternity in 2024 and that some of the men involved were allowed to write essays to mitigate their conduct
U.S. prosecutors reopened an investigation Monday into an alleged gang rape at Cornell University following claims the elite college failed to properly punish the men involved.
The alleged victim said in a civil lawsuit this month she was drugged with ketamine, assaulted and raped in 2024 by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity, a social club for male students.
Cornell closed the fraternity and temporarily suspended the students involved, several of whom were later expelled.
The newly released details of the alleged incident have fuelled allegations that the university was too lenient and reignited a debate over sexual assault on U.S. campuses.
Matthew Van Houten, district attorney for Tompkins County in New York, said that he plans to file criminal charges against the seven men.
He said his office chose in 2024 not to prosecute because the victim’s testimony did not establish a lack of consent, but had now decided to do so in light of her latest allegations.
“I recognize the reality that it can take years of therapy and healing for victims of sexual assaults to fully process and understand what happened to them,” Van Houten said in a statement.
“Seeking justice sometimes requires us to reconsider or reopen cases when we are provided with additional evidence.”
Kyle Kimball, vice president of university relations at Cornell, said the Ivy League school supports the decision to reinvestigate the case.
He also rejected a claim, made in the civil lawsuit, that the suspects were offered the opportunity to write essays to mitigate their conduct.
“Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false,” Kimball said.
The 101-page civil lawsuit filed in New York gives graphic details on the alleged assault of the woman, whose identity is being protected.
Notably, it provides a screenshot of a Snapchat group message advertising “free pussy” during the incident, apparently an invitation for other fraternity members to take part.
The suit seeks financial damages from Cornell and the seven suspects, adding that the woman has suffered “severe emotional and psychological distress.”
British actor Florence Pugh has voiced her anger about the case, saying she felt “uneasy and sick and anxious” after hearing about it.
“Colleges/schools/universities repeatedly fail women around the world,” she wrote on Instagram.
“You build men that get taught through time and time again that they can do extreme harm and that they won’t be harmed in return,” Pugh said.
Prominent Democratic lawmaker Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez condemned a “culture of rape” at elite institutions like Cornell.
“Jane Doe, that survivor, lost her education because you can’t stay in school when something like that happens to you,” Ocasio-Cortez said Sunday.
“She had to lose her education, and those men were protected by an institution and granted an Ivy League degree as a reward. Never again.”

Homes Q&A: What a new Brampton community reveals about solar power
New solar photovoltaic system enables MPV2 condo townhome project to achieve net-zero status while protecting residents against rising rates
We independently select everything we recommend. Buying through us may earn us a commission, which supports our work.
Solar panels are a familiar sight on individual homes, but integrating solar generation across an entire residential community remains relatively uncommon in Canada. A recently completed project in Brampton, however, offers a glimpse of how that could change.
The Daniels Corporation, a Toronto-based housing developer, recently completed a 615-kilowatt DC solar photovoltaic (PV) system at MPV2, a year-old condo townhouse community at Bovaird Drive West and Mississauga Road. The system is owned by AltCrest Energy under an energy-as-a-service model — keep reading for more on that — while Otter Energy handled its engineering, design and construction. The copper-coloured solar panels crown MPV2’s six townhome blocks, which sit next to a pair of condo towers rising 11 and 14 storeys.
Here, Meghan Wilson, Daniels’ senior manager of sustainability, discusses the economics of residential solar, why low- and mid-rise housing is particularly well suited to it, and what developers can do today to prepare homes for a solar-powered future.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
What are the biggest advantages of incorporating solar power into a new residential development?
The big benefit — and really the origin of the solar system at MPV2 — is about enabling homes to be net zero, which means producing as much electricity as you consume. Solar provides that renewable generation.
There’s also a broader benefit to generating electricity on site. As we bring more all-electric communities online, that puts more pressure on the electrical grid. Pairing electrification with on-site solar creates a synergy. You’re helping reduce demand on the grid while also potentially insulating residents against large increases in utility costs over time.
If there are clear benefits, why isn’t community-scale solar more common?
For condos, one of the biggest challenges is the upfront cost. From a developer’s perspective, you typically aren’t maintaining ownership of the solar asset over its entire lifespan, so you don’t necessarily receive the long-term payback that you might under another ownership model.
That’s where the structure we used at MPV2 becomes important. AltCrest owns and operates the solar infrastructure and sells electricity back to the community under a long-term power purchase agreement. Residents benefit from renewable energy, and are protected against rising grid rates, without the condo corporation having to bear the full upfront capital cost.
Are homebuyers actually looking for sustainability features such as solar?
Buyers today are more sophisticated than they were even five years ago, particularly when it comes to specific technologies, sustainability features and available incentives.
But they’re generally looking for outcomes rather than simply a sustainability label. They want lower operating costs and a better experience. That can include improved thermal comfort, greater energy efficiency or better noise isolation through features such as triple-glazed windows.
In a challenging housing market, buyers are paying close attention to value. Delivering a community that goes beyond the basic specification can provide a real advantage.
What made MPV2 particularly well suited to solar?
Sustainability and decarbonization were baked into the vision for the community from the outset. That intentionality made an enormous difference.
For example, we were able to design the rooflines to maximize the number of solar panels. On a retrofit project you might have dormers, irregular roof shapes or other obstructions that make panel placement difficult.

Analysis: B.C. Conservatives get Caroline Elliott after all
‘I don't know if I'm as ambitious as people think,’ Elliott says. ‘I've never felt that it had to be, you know, me at the top of the totem pole’
The tables have turned.
Four months ago, Caroline Elliott lost the B.C. Conservative leadership to Kerry-Lynne Findlay on a 51-49 fourth-ballot runoff. Findlay is gone. Elliott is now on the ballot in West Vancouver-Capilano, her North Shore turf, in the snap election Premier David Eby called for Oct. 24.
“If I was ready to jump in for leadership and lead the party — and ultimately, in an ideal world, the province,” she told me early Monday, “then I should be able to step up for my local riding.”
Eagle-eyed readers will note that I wrote about Elliott just last week, when she hadn’t yet confirmed she was running. She’s an important figure in this election, which is important for B.C., and I wanted to speak with her to follow up.
Lorne Doerkson, the interim leader the party board says will stay on if Conservatives win, gets her “full-hearted endorsement.” I asked, bluntly, about her own ambitions. She lost a knife-edge race to someone who did not last. There is not a whiff of woe-is-me.
“It’s funny,” she says. “I don’t know if I’m as ambitious as people think. I’m really driven on the issues, but if I can drive them in a different way, I’ve never felt that it had to be, you know, me at the top of the totem pole.”
Doerkson, she says, is the right person. “He’s such a good and decent man.” It is not only his legislative and business experience, “he brings an authenticity B.C. is ready for after years of David Eby, who does not present in the same way at all.”
“If he earns a mandate from the public of British Columbia, then I think it would be entirely reasonable for him to say that’s mandate enough to continue leading the party.”
She does not need the title; she wants the files. She is comfortable Doerkson cares about many of the same ones. “I feel pretty comfortable that I’ll be able to pursue those things under his leadership.”

She jumped into this race because commentary — she is a founder of Without Diminishment on Substack and a sometime contributor to National Post — is not the same as a vote in caucus. “I can write about [these issues] all day, I can post videos about them all day, I can speak at events about them all day, but the most effective way, I think, is to have a seat at the table where you’re really driving them.”
“That’s what I want to bring, is that voice at the table, explaining, all the time, the crucial importance of things like: what’s happening in our education system and how important it is when it comes to a whole generation of future citizens; the importance of bringing up things like the criminal justice system, which is more than just a catch-and-release program, there’s an underlying philosophy that’s I think cultural in nature.”
Then there are the Indigenous rights and land files she has been on for years. British Columbians, she says, are nervous about private property after the Cowichan title decision, and they understand the economic bite of DRIPA.
The party wanted her, she says, because those ideas “have a place in the party” — and because she had a lot of support in the leadership race. They want members to see “this party is representative of what they’ve previously voted for or shown interest in.”
She knows voters also want the kitchen-table list. “There’s a crazy cost of living crisis in British Columbia, especially in the Vancouver area,” plus health care and schools. “We’re going to be needing to talk about a range of issues.”

items.title: Ce silence assourdissant de Cris Derksen
items.summary: Une Journée nationale de la vérité et de la réconciliation en mémoire de celle qui devait l’illuminer.
items.body_text:
L’événement musical au Musée des beaux-arts de Montréal dans le cadre de la Journée nationale de la vérité et de la réconciliation, mercredi, devait mettre en valeur une nouvelle création de la violoncelliste et compositrice crie Cris Derksen. La mort accidentelle de la musicienne, le 16 mai dernier, en a décidé autrement. Les concerts seront dédiés à sa mémoire.
Le programme de la salle Bourgie était déjà imprimé avec les photographies de la soprano innue Elisabeth St-Gelais et de la compositrice crie Cris Derksen, lorsque la nouvelle de la mort accidentelle de cette dernière, le 16 mai, à l’âge de 45 ans, au retour de l’enterrement de son père, a glacé d’effroi la communauté musicale.
Directeur artistique de la salle Bourgie, Olivier Godin avait choisi Cris Derksen pour un projet particulier autour de la date du 30 septembre. « C’est une collaboration de la salle Bourgie avec le Festival international de la littérature et Michelle Corbeil, sa directrice, avec qui je travaille régulièrement. C’est un projet que nous avons élaboré en 2023 et que nous voulions répéter cette année en collaboration avec le musée, puisque le concert a lieu dans le musée », nous explique Olivier Godin.
L’idée, à l’occasion de la Journée nationale de la vérité et de la réconciliation, est de demander à un ou une artiste autochtone littéraire de s’intéresser à une œuvre du musée et d’écrire un poème inspiré de l’œuvre choisie. « Ensuite, on demande à un compositeur ou une compositrice des Premières Nations de mettre ça en musique. Cette année, ce devait être Cris Derksen qui mettait en musique un texte de Natasha Kanapé Fontaine », nous dit Olivier Godin.
Retour aux origines
Au moment de la mort de la compositrice, le texte était écrit, mais nul ne connaissait l’état d’avancement de la partition. « Plutôt que de changer de compositrice, nous avons décidé de laisser ce projet-là en plan et de reprendre l’œuvre de 2023, qui n’avait été donnée qu’une seule fois. » Il s’agit, en la matière, d’un poème de Maya Cousineau Mollen, poète innue qui s’est inspirée d’une sculpture de George Segal, Femme assise sur un lit, située dans le Pavillon pour la Paix — dans la section d’art contemporain. « C’est une œuvre très sombre, toute noire, représentant une femme assise sur un lit devant un store noir. Maya a écrit le poème intitulé Rien ne tuera ma lumière, une commande du Festival international de la littérature, et la salle Bourgie en a confié la mise en musique à Barbara Assiginaak. Ça a été composé pour la voix d’Elisabeth St-Gelais, qui chantera l’œuvre directement devant la sculpture dans le Pavillon pour la Paix à trois reprises lors de la Journée de la vérité et de la réconciliation », précise Olivier Godin.
Ces rendez-vous, à 11 h, à 15 h et à 18 h mercredi, sont moins des concerts que des instants de rassemblement. « C’est un moment de réflexion. La manière dont Barbara a mis le texte en musique permet de très bien le comprendre ; on peut vraiment méditer là-dessus. C’est bref, mais c’est un rassemblement où l’on se retrouve avec les gens des Premières Nations pour penser au passé et à l’avenir », résume le directeur artistique de la salle Bourgie. « Lors du premier concert, il y aura évidemment un hommage à Cris Derksen, d’autant que le poème de Maya Cousineau Mollen fait référence à la mort et à la disparition. Barbara Assiginaak sera d’ailleurs là ; elle vient d’Ontario pour l’occasion ; tout s’est effondré quand Cris est décédée, et ça nous a tous bouleversés. »
L’accès au musée sera gratuit à ce moment-là, hors expositions temporaires. Le rendez-vous de 11 h sera ponctué de discours. Ceux de 15 h et de 18 h se résument à la prestation d’Elisabeth St-Gelais avec une petite mise en scène dans une œuvre d’une dizaine de minutes. « C’est très profond, très beau, et ça porte à réfléchir. En 2023, il y avait au moins une centaine de personnes à chaque représentation, avec beaucoup de membres des communautés autochtones », souligne Olivier Godin.
Elisabet
