items.title: China’s economy is changing rapidly. It’s no longer Australia’s easy export market
items.summary: Australian exports to China in three key sectors are all slowing. Businesses will need to meet the challenge.
items.body_text:
For decades, China’s market of 1.4 billion people and extraordinary economic growth gave Australian exporters seemingly endless opportunities. The prevailing assumption was that China’s growing middle class would:
- build more infrastructure requiring steel
- consume more electricity using coal
- and send their children overseas for education.
But China has been transitioning rapidly from the manufacturing powerhouse of the early 2000s. It became an innovation powerhouse in the mid-2010s and established global brands in the past five years. The assumption that Western products and brands would retain an enduring advantage has become outdated.
Australia, as a main beneficiary of China’s growth, needs a strategy for what comes next.
China’s rapid transition
A key driver of China’s rapid transition is the mix of top-down long-term industrial policy and a highly competitive domestic market.
Top-down policy from the Chinese government provides direction and certainty for companies and investors.
They focus on new technologies to decarbonise the economy through renewables, or become a high-tech leader in artificial intelligence (AI), robotics or medicine. Innovation is driven by mostly private companies that make decisions quickly, compete aggressively and collaborate across sectors.
The scale of this effort is considerable. China invested 61% more in research and development in 2025 than it did five years earlier. In 2024, its research spending surpassed that of the United States, adjusted for the purchasing power of different currencies.
By 2025, China’s research and development as a share of economic growth exceeded the average of OECD nations.
The new reality for coal and iron ore
For Australia, which sends about 30% of its total exports to China, this transition is already showing in the numbers for our most important export sectors.
Iron ore is the clearest example. Australian iron ore exports to China, which account for around 15–20% of the nation’s total global exports, have been falling from a peak of A$127 billion in 2021 to A$104 billion in 2025.
China’s steel industry is transitioning to low-carbon iron and steel, driven by tougher regulation and new sources of iron ore.
The iron ore that Australian companies are currently shipping to China does not meet quality standards for low-carbon smelting technologies. To ensure long-term exports continue, Australia will need to invest billions in “green” iron capacity, mainly through renewable energy and processing facilities.
Coal faces a similar challenge. Australian coal exports to China have fallen even more – by as much as 50% since the post-COVID peak in 2024.
This drop has been driven by China adding massive amounts of new solar and wind – about 1,668 gigawatts of energy capacity between 2015 and 2025. This has overtaken coal capacity and led to a decline of coal consumption in 2025.
China will not stop using coal overnight. But Australian exporters must assume that Chinese coal demand will keep falling, even as its energy demand continues to rise.
Student numbers are falling too
Higher education faces a different version of the same problem. Students from mainland China comprised about 43% of Australia’s fee-paying overseas students in 2024.
Yet arrivals of new higher-education students from mainland China fell by 18% in 2025–26 due to an ageing Chinese population with fewer students, and, importantly, fewer benefits from studying in Australia.
In the 2025 rankings of global research institutions published by Nature, mainland Chinese institutions held nine of the top 10 positions, up from just one in 2020. On that ranking, Monash University, Australia’s highest-ranked institution, placed 113th – trailing 55 Chinese institutions.
For many Chinese students and families, the question is why study abroad if studying in China is deepening knowledge and local networks relevant for jobs, while Australia makes the pathway to residency more difficult?

items.title: Stripped titles? Compensating rivals? How the Manchester City cheating scandal could play out
items.summary: Manchester City could be facing enormous sanctions for cheating – and the fallout may spread to its 13 teams around the world, from New York to Melbourne.
items.body_text:
One of the biggest cheating scandals in world sports history has erupted in England: Manchester City has reportedly been found guilty of 114 of the 115 alleged breaches of English Premier League financial rules brought against the club in 2023.
The charges relate to the club’s incredibly successful spell between 2009 and 2018 when they won seven major titles, headlined by three Premier League championships.
Manchester City was bought in 2008 by the Abu Dhabi United Group, led by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan – a member of the Abu Dhabi royal family.
The group now owns or has a stake in 13 football teams across the world, from New York to Melbourne, meaning there may be ramifications well beyond England.
But Manchester City is expected to appeal, having long protested its innocence – so this case is not over yet.
What are the charges?
The guilty findings are a potentially seismic development in a case that has hung over English football for more than three years.
The charges cover several areas, including:
- the accuracy of financial information supplied to the Premier League
- player and manager remuneration
- compliance with Union of European Football Associations (UEFA) and Premier League financial regulations
- cooperation with the league’s investigation.
But there are important caveats. The independent commission’s decision has not yet been published, no sanction has been announced, Manchester City has consistently denied wrongdoing – which is why an appeal is expected.
Until the written decision is available, any assessment of precisely what City did and what should happen next would be premature.
What could happen to Manchester City?
Recent Premier League cases demonstrate how breaches of financial rules can result in sporting sanctions.
In recent years, Everton was initially deducted ten points (reduced to six points on appeal) for breaching the league’s Profitability and Sustainability Rules, while Nottingham Forest was deducted four points. Both sides narrowly avoided relegation after the sanctions.
But these cases provide limited guidance for Manchester City. They concerned relatively discrete breaches of spending rules, whereas the charges against City cover multiple categories of alleged misconduct over almost a decade.
So any attempt to extrapolate a likely points deduction for City from Everton or Forest would be speculative.
More severe possibilities – including relegation or expulsion from the Premier League – have inevitably been discussed, as has the prospect of retrospectively stripping City of titles.
Little precedent exists for the latter in English professional team sport. Saracens were relegated from rugby union’s Premiership following salary-cap breaches in 2020, but their previously won titles were not removed.
Australian sport, however, provides precedent. The National Rugby League (NRL) stripped the Melbourne Storm of their 2007 and 2009 premierships, three minor premierships, and all their 2010 competition points after it uncovered systematic salary cap breaches.
Those cases illustrate possible sporting sanctions. But they cannot establish what City’s penalty should be before the commission publishes its reasoning.
Could the consequences spread beyond Manchester?
The shockwaves from this case could also spread overseas.
The City Football Group owns or has a stake in 13 clubs worldwide – including Melbourne City, New York City and Italy’s Palermo.
For example, Melbourne City joined City Football Group in 2014 and is now wholly owned by it.
A Premier League sanction against the English team would not automatically apply to the Melbourne club.
Yet if the published findings concern governance, financial reporting or transactions within the wider ownership structure, they may prompt scrutiny of how the group oversees its international clubs.

items.body_text:
UK accused of 'fuelling' Yemen war as Saudi jets receive British support
The UK government faces calls to halt military support for Saudi Arabia as fighting escalates in Yemen, with academics and civil society organisations warning that British refuelling for Saudi fighter jets could make it complicit in further violations of international law.
In an open letter addressed to Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, the signatories said they were “deeply concerned” about the decision to refuel Royal Saudi Air Force aircraft as hostilities escalate in and around Yemen.
“There is a real risk that further UK military support for Saudi Arabia will not achieve the desired outcome and could make the UK complicit in further war crimes and violations of international humanitarian law,” they wrote.
The Campaign Against Arms Trade, Action on Armed Violence, Shadow World Investigations UK and the Yemen Relief and Reconstruction Foundation signed the letter alongside academics and specialists in international relations, human rights and international law.
The signatories highlighted longstanding British support for Saudi military action in Yemen, which began in 2015 and initially involved a coalition of Arab states.

Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
The Yemen Data Project recorded 25,054 Saudi-led coalition air raids between 2015 and 2022, according to figures cited in the letter. The organisations said extensive evidence showed that the air campaign attacked civilians and civilian infrastructure.
The war also combined an air and sea blockade with economic collapse and ground fighting. The UN Development Programme estimated that the conflict killed 377,000 people directly and indirectly by the end of 2021, the letter said.
The signatories also cited allegations that the Saudi-led coalition used starvation as a weapon during the conflict.
'Risking complicity'
The groups argue that the Saudi-led intervention failed to defeat or dislodge the Houthis, who continued to control most of Yemen's population.
They also criticised Britain's role in US air strikes against the Houthis in spring 2025. The UK reportedly supported those operations by providing refuelling.
The signatories cited a Pentagon assessment that said the strikes between March and May 2025 “more likely than not” caused 281 civilian casualties.
The latest escalation has unfolded against a wider regional crisis.
The letter cites reports that fighting has displaced around 130,000 people in recent weeks. It also says the violence has already caused 110 casualties, including 28 deaths.
The signatories also raised concerns about Houthi attacks and attempted attacks on civilian infrastructure in Saudi Arabia.
They attributed the latest escalation to several factors, including developments inside Yemen, the US-Israeli war on Iran and the war in Gaza.
But the groups argue that more air strikes will not resolve the conflict.
“Past experience has shown that air strikes will not contribute to defeating the Houthis or alleviating pressure on Saudi Arabia or on global shipping routes,” they wrote.
“Instead, the UK is only further fuelling the war and is risking complicity in further crimes.”
'De-escalatory diplomacy'
The organisations called on the British government to stay out of Saudi military operations and pursue diplomatic efforts to de-escalate the conflict.

“In light of Saudi Arabia’s extensive record of violations in Yemen, we urge your government not to involve itself in Saudi operations and focus on de-escalatory diplomacy,” they wrote.

items.body_text:
Gaza officials warn of imminent 'humanitarian catastrophe' as winter approaches
Gaza’s Government Media Office has accused Israel of violating its commitments under the Gaza ceasefire agreement, saying the continued violations have worsened the humanitarian crisis as the ceasefire approaches its first anniversary.
Israel had committed 5,147 violations that killed 1,421 Palestinians, injured 4,983 and caused the arrest of 198 people, the office said.
It also said 72,826 aid trucks had entered Gaza of an expected 210,600 under the agreement, while only 13,785 people had been allowed to travel in and out of the territory of an expected 35,000.
As winter approaches, the office warned of a “certain humanitarian catastrophe” as more than 1.5 million displaced Palestinians live in worn-out tents.
It said 162,000 of Gaza’s estimated 270,000 tents were already unusable and warned that more than 255 damaged buildings were in danger of collapse.
The office appealed to the international community and the UN agencies to intervene urgently, fully open Gaza’s crossings, facilitate medical evacuations and allow winter relief supplies into the territory.

items.title: Pope wraps up four-day visit to France with call for European peace and unity
items.summary: Speaking at an interfaith meeting in Metz, he urged religious leaders to foster a path to friendship, peace, and brotherhood.
items.body_text:
France
On the last day of his four-day visit to France on Monday, Catholic Pope Leo XIV condemned any use of God’s name to justify violence and oppression.
“Invoking God’s name to legitimise violence or oppression is a desecration of that name. Nothing that undermines human dignity can claim to be genuinely inspired by God,” he said.
Speaking at an interfaith meeting in Metz, he urged the various religious leaders to foster a path to friendship, peace, and brotherhood.
The eastern city, near the border with Luxembourg and Germany, is closely linked to Robert Schuman, one of the founding fathers of the European Union.
Leo spoke of the forces of dialogue that contributed to Europe’s post-World War II integration, saying it should remember this tradition when confronting today’s challenges of war, migration, and polarisation.
“Dialogue does not diminish our identity but expresses it with simplicity and truth by opening us to the difference of the other,” he said.
Leo said that religion cannot be used to justify violence in a world market by conflict and contempt for the most vulnerable.
“Religious discourse must constantly call for the disarming of hearts and words. This entails the direct responsibility of each of us, as guardians of our respective traditions,” he said.
Religions must protect human dignity and be “protect, accompany, and serve life”, he said, adding it was always possible to come together across borders and build peace.

items.title: South Africa: Competition between criminal networks fuelling mass shootings, analysts say
items.summary: Organised crime, gang violence and conflicts over the control of criminal networks are fuelling mass shootings in South Africa, according to the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime.
items.body_text:
South Africa
Organised crime, gang violence and conflicts over the control of criminal networks are fuelling mass shootings in South Africa, according to the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC).
Since the start of 2026, South Africa has recorded 41 mass shootings, resulting in almost 200 deaths, according to data from the GI-TOC. The organisation defines a mass shooting as an incident where at least three people are killed.
Shootings in Johannesburg and Cape Town last weekend saw 27 deaths in just two days.
Just days earlier, 12 people - including a pregnant woman - were killed south of Durban when gunmen stormed a house.
Much of this violence is linked to competition between criminal networks and individuals looking to control illicit markets, the GI-TOC says.
The rise in mass shootings comes as overall crime statistics show a different trend.
The latest quarterly data from the South African police indicate an almost 6 percent drop in homicides between April and June.

items.title: Morocco detains Tangier mayor over alleged electoral fraud
items.summary: The mayor of Tangier, Mounir Limouri, was placed in police custody on Monday over alleged electoral fraud in the recent parliamentary elections.
items.body_text:
Morocco
Moroccan authorities on Monday placed the mayor of Tangier in police custody over suspected electoral fraud in the recent parliamentary elections, a judicial source told AFP.
Five other people, including two officials who were overseeing polling stations in Tangier, were "being held in pre-trial detention", also over electoral fraud accusations, the source who spoke on condition of anonymity said.
Mayor Mounir Limouri "was placed in police custody by order of the public prosecutor's office as part of the investigation into suspected electoral fraud", the source added.
Morocco's ruling coalition dominated the parliamentary election last week, but the poll was marked by the lowest turnout in two decades and reports of ballot fraud in Tangier.
The interior ministry said that a sweeping investigation into the reports was ongoing.
Media reports said Limouri was detained upon arrival at Tangier airport from Spain, following a warrant issued against him for the alleged tampering of ballots in his constituency.
One polling station official in the northern city was arrested the day of the vote, after he was allegedly found with documents meant for ballot tampering, according to media reports.
Limouri, a member of the centre-right Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) which won the election, told news website Le360 over the weekend that he "had no connection" with the incident.
The PAM won 97 out of 395 seats in the House of Representatives, while the National Rally of Independents (RNI), which heads the outgoing coalition, came in second with 66 seats.
Morocco is set to appoint its next prime minister from the PAM, with Fouzi Lekjaa — who serves as budget minister and is better known as chief of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation — likely to be tapped as premier.
But Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri, the PAM's national coordinator who serves as the current territorial planning minister and mayor of Marrakesh, could also be in line to become Morocco's first woman prime minister.

items.summary: Could the conventionally-powered KSS-III sub offer a more affordable and timely alternative to the planned nuclear-powered fleet?
items.body_text:
In July, the Canadian government announced that it has chosen the German-Norwegian bid to build 12 conventionally-powered submarines to replace their obsolete Victoria class fleet. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation reported the estimated cost of the submarines at CA$24 billion. With 35-year lifetime maintenance and sustainment costs added, the overall program cost is likely to be in the vicinity of CA$100 billion. This compares more than favorably to the A$368 billion (the dollar equivalents are similar) allocated so far to AUKUS.
The Canadians said they had a hard time choosing between two excellent options – the other being the South Korean KSS-III submarine.
Professor Hugh White has long experience with our Collins class submarine project and, more recently, with the details of AUKUS. He says that as an alternative to the AUKUS project “any off-the-shelf submarines Australia could get its hands on, we should take.”
One option is to turn back to the French Naval Group for a new order of 12 submarines. In evidence given to the AUKUS public inquiry in Canberra on 2 September, retired admiral Peter Briggs gave an informed presentation on the capabilities of nuclear-powered submarines. He favors procurement of a low-enriched uranium nuclear-powered submarine, based on the French Suffren class, for the Royal Australian Navy (RAN). He strongly opposes purchase of the US Virginia class and the proposed British-designed SSN AUKUS boats, describing the plan as “flawed and undeliverable”.
His conclusion about the AUKUS submarines is widely supported by the evidence and a strong consensus of military and academic opinion.
During his presentation Admiral Briggs stated his view that conventional diesel-electric submarine technology was not acceptable for the next generation of RAN operations. His argument was that conventionally powered submarines have neither the stealth features nor the endurance needed for effective undersea naval operations. Nonetheless, the example he cited concerned the limitations of the existing Collins class submarine design. As is well known, Collins is an outdated platform that is nearing the end of its operational life.
Given the South Koreans only recently lost the bid for 12 submarines to replace the ageing Canadian fleet, their new submarine should be available for export without delay. The KSS-III proposal had an appealing range of handover deadlines promised for Canada. The expected first boat delivery date was scheduled to be 2032, with the initial batch of four submarines delivered by 2035 and the remaining eight boats at the rate of one per year until 2043, when the entire fleet of 12 would be in service. It has been reported that the South Korean tender may have suffered a disadvantage because Canadian infrastructure and crew capacity to absorb the fleet in that timeframe is underdeveloped. This is much less a problem in Australia.
These delivery timeframes compare to 2032 proposed for the first second-hand AUKUS Virginia; thereafter delivery in 2035 and 2038 respectively. The first British-designed AUKUS SSN boat is not expected to be delivered until the fuzzy “2040s.” Obviously, procurement of an entire one-class fleet of 12 KSS-III submarines by 2043 is an attractive option. It would adequately cover the capability gap of decommissioned Collins class submarines, scheduled to begin in 2040. If the argument about needing more naval capability now has any relevance, early delivery is a must.

items.title: Vietnam Confirms Arrest of Viet Tan Activists Reported Missing in Cambodia
items.summary: Rights groups claim that Nguyen Duc Thuan and Tran Hiep were abducted in Cambodia, in line with a pattern of growing transnational repression by the Vietnamese state.
items.body_text:
Vietnam has confirmed the arrest of two activists, reported missing in neighboring Cambodia earlier this month, whom rights group claim were abducted by the Vietnamese authorities.
The Ministry of Public Security said yesterday that its Security Investigation Agency had detained three men after they “entered Vietnam illegally from Cambodia,” the state-run newspaper Tuoi Tre reported.
Nguyen Duc Thuan, 52, Ho Pham Hiep Huy (also known as Tran Hiep), 51, and Thai Cong Truong Son, 46, are under investigation for “Terrorism” under Article 299 of the Penal Code and “Forging seals and documents of agencies and organizations” under Article 341.
Under questioning, the three confessed to being members of Viet Tan, a U.S.-based pro-democracy group that the Ministry described as a “terrorist organization.” It said that they also admitted to “carrying fake documents to illegally enter Việt Nam to conduct terrorist and sabotage activities.”
The Ministry’s announcement came after Thuan and Hiep corresponded with two political activists who were reported missing in Phnom Penh by Viet Tan earlier this month. In an alert dated September 25, the organization, which says that it advocates a “peaceful, nonviolent struggle” for democracy in Vietnam, said that the two men had been missing in Cambodia since September 18.
Thuan, a Norwegian citizen, and Hiep, an Australian citizen, had arrived in Phnom Penh from Bangkok on September 15 and were due to leave Cambodia on September 19, but never boarded their flights, Viet Tan spokesperson Duy Hoang told Cambodia’s Kiripost news site. Hoang added that the pair came to Cambodia to meet with Vietnamese human rights defenders who lived in the country.
Viet Tan, which was formed by South Vietnamese exiles in 1982, is high on the hitlist of the communist authorities, who remain paranoid about any advocacy that is even tangentially linked to the cause of the defunct southern Republic of Vietnam.
After the arrest of the pair, Viet Tan accused the Vietnamese authorities of abducting Thuan and Hiep from Cambodia.
“Viet Tan strongly condemns the abduction of two of its members in Cambodia and the fabricated charges issued by the Vietnamese communist authorities to cover up an act of transnational repression,” it said in a statement yesterday. The Ministry of Public’s Security’s claim that the two men were arrested for entering Vietnam illegally was a “a blatant fabrication intended to conceal the fact that the Viet Tan members were abducted in Cambodia and forcibly taken to Vietnam,” it added.
According to rights groups, these sorts of renditions are part of a worrying trend under To Lam, a former minister of public security who has significantly tightened the bound of permissible dissent since his appointment as chief of the Communist Party of Vietnam in 2024. In a report released last week, Viet Tan documented 20 cases “in which Vietnamese authorities have pursued critics and human rights defenders beyond Vietnam’s borders” in recent years.
According to the report, the trend marks “a new phase” in Hanoi’s security strategy. It argued that “repression is no longer confined to Vietnamese territory, but increasingly targets political exiles, refugees, bloggers, human rights defenders, and members of the Vietnamese diaspora residing in democratic countries.
Indeed, the case of Thuan and Hiep bears a close resemblance to that of Duong Van Thai, a prominent Vietnamese blogger and YouTuber who fled to Thailand in 2018. In April 2023, Thai went missing unexpectedly after he left his rental home in Bangkok to pick up a friend at the airport. Several days later, Vietnamese police announced that he had been arrested for entering the country illegally from Laos in similar circumstances to this week’s case. Rights groups including Viet Tan say that Thai was abducted by or on behalf of the Vietnamese government.
The following year, Thai was sentenced to 12 years in prison on charges of publishing anti-state propaganda.

items.title: The Global Data Center Boom Has Arrived in Southeast Asia
items.summary: Will the region's demand for artificial intelligence services justify the enormous outlays of money and resources?
items.body_text:
Processing and storing data is now pushing the frontier of economic development around the world, and huge amounts of capital are flowing into building out the infrastructure to support this big bet on cloud computing and Artificial Intelligence. The race to establish an advantageous position on the digital frontier is driving a major capex boom in the United States and elsewhere, and this wave has now fully arrived in Southeast Asia.
Data centers require substantial land and resources, like electricity and water, and they need reliable connectivity such as access to subsea cable networks. Countries that have land, reasonably well-developed energy and telecommunications infrastructure and friendly regulatory environments are attracting investors and developers looking to ride the data center wave. Affordable inputs, like electricity, can sweeten the deal. It just so happens that many countries in Southeast Asia fit this bill.
Malaysia is leading the pack. Clear policy guidance, well-developed infrastructure and close proximity to land-constrained Singapore are helping fuel a boom in data centers. The Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone has seen a flurry of activity, but it is part of a broader phenomenon. In the first quarter of 2023, the Department of Statistics recorded a cumulative $11 billion of foreign investment in the information and communication sector, accounting for 5 percent of total foreign investment. By first quarter of 2026, this figure had risen to $32.5 billion, equal to 12 percent of total inbound investment.
And there is no sign of slowing. According to the Malaysian Investment Development Authority, the body that reviews and approves investment projects, between 2021 and the first quarter of 2026, $96 billion worth of data center and cloud computing projects were approved, including $24 billion in the first half of 2026 alone. These are project approvals rather than realized investment, but it gives a sense of the speed and scale at which the data center boom is unfolding across Malaysia.
Indonesia is also seeing an uptick in data center investment. Like Malaysia, some of this is driven by demand from Singapore, particularly in and around the island of Batam. Nongsa Digital Park is a Special Economic Zone that offers eligible projects tax and other fiscal incentives. Combined with Batam’s strong subsea cable connectivity, this has fueled a wave of new data center construction in the area.
There is also a lot of investment activity in and around Jakarta where a number of large industrial scale data centers are being developed by state-backed players such as Telkom, as well as private sector firms and investors. As reported by Antara News, Indonesia’s current data center capacity sits around 580 MW and the plan is to grow it to 1.3 GW in the near-term. Government data shows that investment in information services jumped from $967 million in 2023 to $3.4 billion in 2025 and it looks set to keep climbing.
Thailand is also now rushing to add more data centers, with several large industrial-scale projects in the pipeline. According to the Board of Investment, in 2025 they received $24 billion worth of applications across 151 projects in the digital industry, mainly data centers. Not all of these projects will be approved and become operational, but it again gives a sense of the speed and scale with which this industry is moving. Vietnam is following suit, with local media reporting that the government plans to reach 870 MW of data center capacity by 2030.
The trend is clear: data centers are beginning to pop up all around Southeast Asia, attracting billions of dollars in investment and uncorking a major construction boom. items.title: Bangladesh energy crisis calls for pragmatism, not political purity
items.summary: For more than three decades, the Bangladeshi political left has maintained an unyielding stance on natural resources like gas, coal, and minerals, insisting that state entities must develop them exclusively. Foreign energy companies are viewed with deep suspicion, while production-sharing contracts are routinely condemned as vehicles designed to siphon national wealth to foreign multinationals. Coal […] The post Bangladesh energy crisis calls for pragmatism, not political purity appeared first o
items.body_text:
For more than three decades, the Bangladeshi political left has maintained an unyielding stance on natural resources like gas, coal, and minerals, insisting that state entities must develop them exclusively.
Foreign energy companies are viewed with deep suspicion, while production-sharing contracts are routinely condemned as vehicles designed to siphon national wealth to foreign multinationals. Coal extraction, particularly open-pit mining, has drawn even sharper resistance.
Few figures have championed this doctrine more consistently than economist Anu Muhammad and his National Committee to Protect Oil, Gas, Mineral Resources, Power and Ports. Their long-standing campaigns have influenced the nation’s media narrative on energy.
By transforming projects like the Phulbari open-pit coal mine into lightning rods for outrage, they have successfully framed energy deals with outside capital as existential threats to national ownership.
To be sure, their environmental objections warrant rigorous examination. The Phulbari dispute raised acute questions regarding mass human displacement, farmland destruction, groundwater depletion and ecological ruin.
As Anu Muhammad reaffirmed recently, resource extraction cannot be plausibly classified as development if it dismantles local agrarian economies, ecosystems and human habitations.
Yet the left’s stance becomes intellectually fragile when legitimate environmental advocacy hardens into an indiscriminate hostility toward foreign capital and technical expertise. Bangladesh can no longer afford to treat its national energy discourse as an abstract seminar or a street protest over political purity.
The country faces an acute energy crisis. Daily gas demand is around 3,800 to 4,000 million cubic feet, while domestic production provides barely 2,600 million. Shrinking domestic reserves have forced the state into dangerous over-reliance on imported liquefied natural gas (LNG).
This import dependency has proven very costly. Recent geopolitical volatility across Middle Eastern supply routes has pushed Asian spot LNG prices to eye-watering highs.
Bangladeshi manufacturers now endure persistent supply curtailments and rolling power outages, while the treasury absorbs sharp fiscal burdens. Over 40% of the nation’s power generation currently hinges on imported LNG, severely undercutting industrial expansion.
This is why the old dogma on foreign exploration must be re-evaluated. Left-wing commentators persistently offer BAPEX, the state-owned exploration entity, as a viable solution.
Strengthening state capabilities is undoubtedly a worthy goal; BAPEX possesses valuable localized geological insight, technical personnel and operational infrastructure. But bolstering a national oil company is fundamentally distinct from shutting out global energy corporations.
Consider deep-sea exploration in the Bay of Bengal. High-seas drilling demands immense capital expenditure alongside extreme financial risk. A single offshore exploratory well can easily absorb hundreds of millions of dollars without yielding any commercial discoveries.
While nationalizing that risk carries rhetorical political appeal, the state remains fully exposed when costly wells come up dry. International oil majors exist precisely because their global balance sheets can absorb such losses.
Bangladesh has spent years learning how challenging it is to lure global energy majors. Despite restructuring production-sharing terms to offer lucrative blocks across the Bay of Bengal, major tenders have repeatedly failed to attract a single international bid.
Rather than triggering a serious debate regarding contractual competitiveness, geological data sharing and regulatory predictability, public discourse predictably degenerated into binary slogans pitting national sovereignty against foreign exploitation.

items.title: Indonesia should have a seat at new forest firefighting fund
items.summary: Two American charities recently announced a new fund to fight forest fires. They want to raise US$100 million to help countries find fires faster and put them out sooner. But the fund, announced at the UN General Assembly, is limited to South America, home to the Amazon rainforest. Southeast Asia is left out, and so […] The post Indonesia should have a seat at new forest firefighting fund appeared first on Asia Times.
items.body_text:
Two American charities recently announced a new fund to fight forest fires. They want to raise US$100 million to help countries find fires faster and put them out sooner. But the fund, announced at the UN General Assembly, is limited to South America, home to the Amazon rainforest.
Southeast Asia is left out, and so is Indonesia. Indonesia should not accept this quietly. The government in Jakarta should ask to join the fund and push for it to protect Indonesian forests, too.
The fund began in New York during a major annual climate meeting. Two nonprofit groups, Renaissance Philanthropy and Conservation X Labs, lead it. The Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation gave $30 million, and the David and Lucile Packard Foundation added $5 million.
The plan copies what already works, such as a camera network in Brazil that spots smoke early and a team of Indigenous firefighters in Bolivia that has worked for 15 years. Indonesia needs these ideas right now.
This year has been hard for Indonesia. Government data shows that fires burned more than 202,000 hectares of land from January to June, and almost 95,000 more hectares in July alone.
In half a year, the country lost an area nearly three times the size of Singapore. In West Kalimantan, smoke covered the city of Pontianak so thickly that it was almost invisible from the air. Schools closed, and flights were delayed. People in Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei and the Philippines breathed the smoke too.
The Center of Economic and Law Studies, a research group in Jakarta, estimates that fires from January to August cost Indonesia between 40 and 123 trillion rupiah in lost business and health care. In 2015, the World Bank calculated that fires cost the country $16 billion. That was more than twice the money needed to rebuild Aceh after the 2004 tsunami.
Why are Indonesia’s fires so hard to stop? A big part of the answer is peat. Peat is soft, wet soil made from dead plants that pile up over thousands of years. Indonesia holds about 36% of the world’s tropical peat.
When peat dries out, fire can spread underground, where water dropped from planes cannot reach it. This year, El Niño, a change in ocean temperature that brings long dry months to the region, has made the drought worse.
Some people will say the fund was made for the Amazon and Indonesia should solve its own problems. I disagree, for three reasons.
The first reason is money. In the same week, a United Nations report found that the world needs $66.8 billion more by 2030 to protect tropical forests. In 2023, only $14.6 billion was spent.
Almost 80% of the rainforest left on Earth is in three places: the Amazon, the Congo Basin in Africa, and Borneo, the island Indonesia shares with Malaysia and Brunei. If donors build a fire fund for only one of these places, the other two will keep waiting. Leaving out Southeast Asia was a big mistake.
The second reason is that Indonesia has something to offer. Indonesia has fought peat fires for about 30 years. Its Forestry Ministry tracks fire spots almost as they happen, using data from American satellites.
Brazil and Bolivia can learn from Indonesia’s mistakes, and Indonesia can learn from their cameras and their Indigenous fire teams. A fund that connects the Amazon and Borneo will be smarter than one that looks at only one region.
The third reason is harder to say, but it matters most. Most of Indonesia’s fires are started by people. Farmers and companies often burn land because it is the cheapest way to clear it for palm oil, other crops or mines.
If Indonesia joins an international fund, partners will ask difficult questions. The government should welcome these questions. Clear data and fair courts will bring in more support than excuses.
Bambang Hero Saharjo, who leads a fire management center for Southeast Asia, asked the world to help Indonesia put out its fires. But help rarely comes to a country that waits quietly for it.
So what should Jakarta do? The Forestry Ministry and the Foreign Ministry

items.summary: In a recent phone call, Donald Trump urged Volodymyr Zelensky to stop Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. Whether a request or a demand, this appears, certainly at first glance, fundamentally different from the Biden administration’s policy of restricting the use of US long-range missiles to hit targets inside Russia. The US president has justified […] The post Trump’s bid to stop Ukraine’s Russia strikes a strategic disconnect appeared first on Asia Times.
items.body_text:
In a recent phone call, Donald Trump urged Volodymyr Zelensky to stop Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. Whether a request or a demand, this appears, certainly at first glance, fundamentally different from the Biden administration’s policy of restricting the use of US long-range missiles to hit targets inside Russia.
The US president has justified his position primarily on economic grounds. He argues that the regular attacks on Russian refining capacity were contributing to disruptions in diesel supplies and rising fuel prices. The International Energy Agency has estimated that Ukraine hit one Russian oil refinery every three days over the first eight months of 2026.
Joe Biden’s restrictions, by contrast, were justified by the US largely over concerns about military escalation and the possibility that strikes deep inside Russia could provoke a wider confrontation between Moscow and NATO.
But focusing solely on these stated justifications hides a deeper continuity. Both policies reflect an effort by Washington to shape the boundaries of Ukraine’s military response to suit broader American interests.
The significance of this becomes clear when considering Ukraine’s refinery approach. Kyiv’s systematic campaign to target Russian oil infrastructure is about reducing Russia’s economic and military capacity. Ukrainian officials have described the attacks as part of a calculated strategy to reduce Russia’s economic potential.
These attacks were not symbolic. Refineries produce the gasoline, diesel and aviation fuel that support both military and civilian activity. This makes them a logical target within a strategy of economic warfare.
And the strategy has borne fruit. The IEA report found that “gasoline output is down by 20% compared with 2025 levels, while diesel production is estimated to have fallen by nearly 30%.”
From a Ukrainian perspective, these refinery strikes are a strategically valuable means of imposing costs on Russia without requiring costly and large-scale offensive operations along the front.
This context is important because it highlights what is actually at stake in Trump’s efforts to halt the campaign. It was not directed at an ineffective or indiscriminate form of violence. It was aimed at one of Ukraine’s more successful campaigns against Russian infrastructure.
Zelensky reportedly rejected Trump’s request, telling the Wall Street Journal’s editor-in-chief, Emma Tucker, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly meeting on September 23, that “our lives are more important than the price of energy.”
The disagreement between the two leaders reflects their competing conceptions of strategic success. For Zelensky, disrupting Russian refining capacity weakens the economic foundations of Russia’s war effort. For Trump, the same attacks allegedly generate undesirable consequences in the form of higher energy prices and fuel shortages.
The question is not whether the strikes matter – but which effects should be prioritized: pressure on Russia or stability in global energy markets?
What this tells us about US foreign policy
This reveals an important theoretical point about escalation and restraint. Biden’s restrictions reflected a traditional understanding of escalation rooted in military interaction between major powers.
For Biden, the danger lay in provoking Russian retaliation against a backdrop of Russian threats to retaliate with nuclear weapons – or creating the perception of direct US involvement in attacks on Russian territory.
Trump’s position points to a broader conception of escalation by not being limited to Russia itself, but rather where economic interdependence constitutes its own pathway of strategic risk. Refinery attacks may not increase the likelihood of direct military confrontation.
But they can create consequences that spread through global energy markets and generate political costs for governments far removed from the battlefield as they are threatening to do by raising fuel

items.title: Sudan demands UN action against external backers of rebels
items.summary: Sudan has urged pressure on foreign backers of the RSF and accused the UN Security Council of failing to act Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Sudan demands UN action against external backers of rebels
Sudan has called for international action against foreign parties supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) opposing the government, and accused the UN Security Council of failing to identify and condemn the group’s sponsors.
Sudanese Foreign Minister Mohieldin Salim Ahmed Ibrahim made the appeal at the UN General Assembly in New York on Monday, saying external support for the RSF was prolonging the war.
“Pressure must be exerted on the regional sponsors and certain neighboring states,” Ibrahim said.
The foreign minister accused unnamed countries of allowing weapons and supplies to reach the RSF through their territory and enabling attacks by the paramilitary group and mercenaries to be launched from outside Sudan’s borders. He also claimed hospitals had been established in neighboring states to treat wounded RSF fighters.
Ibrahim said the UN Security Council had failed to identify and condemn the RSF’s sponsors, which he accused of recruiting foreign mercenaries, providing political backing to the paramilitary group and financing media platforms spreading what he described as “disinformation” against the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF).
Sudan has previously accused the United Arab Emirates (UAE) of providing military support to the RSF, allegations Abu Dhabi has repeatedly denied. Khartoum has also accused neighboring Ethiopia of allowing its territory to be used for drone attacks against Sudan, a claim Addis Ababa has rejected.
The accusations come weeks after a UN fact-finding mission found reasonable grounds to believe that a transnational network had supplied the RSF with weapons, logistics, training and foreign personnel. Investigators identified private entities and intermediaries operating from countries including the UAE, with transit routes through Chad, southeastern Libya and Somalia.
Ibrahim said peace would require the RSF to be disarmed and its weapons to remain under the control of state institutions. He also called for attacks on civilians and infrastructure to end.
Sudan plunged into a civil war three years ago after a struggle for power broke out between the SAF and the RSF.
Sudan descended into chaos in April 2023 when fighting erupted between the national army (Sudanese Armed Forces, SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). This occurred after months of tension between their commanders, army generals Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo ‘Hemedti’, respectively, over a planned transition to civilian rule. What began in the capital, Khartoum, as a power struggle has devastated the country, killing tens of thousands and displacing millions.
Regional and international peace efforts, including African Union mediation and Saudi–US talks in Jeddah, have repeatedly stalled. Sudanese officials have named Colombians and Ukrainians among mercenaries backing the RSF against the army. Officials have also accused Ukraine and the United Arab Emirates of involvement and recently claimed the European Union has an “incomplete understanding of the complex situation” in the country.
Khartoum has also accused authorities in neighboring Kenya of backing the RSF and has broken ties with the East African grouping IGAD amid mistrust of regional mediation. In July, TASIS, a political coalition aligned with the paramilitary, announced the formation of a rival government months after its members signed a charter in Nairobi. It named Gen. Dagalo as chairman of a 15-member presidential council, a move rejected by the UN and AU.
The RSF was originally established by the Sudanese government under former President Omar al-Bashir in 2013, drawing heavily on the Janjaweed militias that Khartoum had used to fight rebels in Darfur. Its status was later formalized by law before tensions with the regular army erupted into open warfare.

items.title: Dozens of human skulls found in Nigerian forests (VIDEO)
items.summary: Nigerian police have recovered 28 skulls from forest hideouts in Abia State as fresh mass kidnappings are reported elsewhere in the country Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Dozens of human skulls found in Nigerian forests (VIDEO)
At least 28 skulls of suspected kidnap victims have been recovered from outlaw forest hideouts in southeastern Nigeria, the African nation’s law enforcement authorities have reported.
Police found the skulls and other bones during raids on Saturday in the Umuaku and Nneato forests of Abia State. The suspects fled before officers could arrest them, police spokesperson Maureen Chinaka said.
“The criminal camps were subsequently dismantled. Investigation is ongoing, while monitoring of the area continues, and efforts are intensified to apprehend the fleeing suspects,” Chinaka said in a statement.
The remains were found during a weekend of mass abductions elsewhere in Africa’s most populous nation. Armed men seized at least 47 farmers harvesting peanuts in Niger State on Saturday, while about 40 women were kidnapped in neighboring Zamfara on Sunday, AFP reported, citing security reports and a local source. The Nigerian Army said it foiled two other abduction attempts in Zamfara on Sunday and rescued 10 people.
Nigeria has faced a security crisis for more than a decade, marked by kidnappings by jihadist groups and armed gangs. Boko Haram, its Islamic State-linked offshoot Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), and Ansaru have abducted civilians, while gangs locally known as bandits seize people for ransom, particularly in the northwest and north-central regions. Security consultancy SBM Intelligence recorded 7,825 people abducted nationwide between July 2025 and June 2026, a 66% rise on the previous year.
The police raids in Abia took place in Umunneochi district, where gunmen have targeted travelers and residents for years. The state government ordered more checkpoints and told people living in the forests to leave after the kidnapping of Methodist Church leader Samuel Kanu-Uche there in 2022.
A local archbishop described Umunneochi at the time as a “money making center for kidnappers.”
The violence has continued despite a nationwide security emergency declared by President Bola Tinubu, the recruitment of more police personnel and forest guards, and increased security cooperation with the US.
Around 200 American troops were deployed to Nigeria in February to support counterterrorism operations. Most have since withdrawn, and Nigeria said the main force was expected to leave by the end of September, with a smaller advisory team remaining.
US Africa Command called the mission a success, saying a joint operation killed Abu-Bilal al-Minuki and other senior Islamic State figures and disrupted the group’s wider network. Nigerian opposition politician Samuel Memeh disagreed, telling RT the deployment “has not yielded significant improvements” in security.

items.title: Controversy over $62 bn Kenyan rare earth tender
items.summary: Kenya’s tender for a rare earth deposit sought by US and Chinese firms has drawn scrutiny over the absence of an economic viability study Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Controversy over $62 bn Kenyan rare earth tender
Kenya’s political opposition has pushed back against a government tender for a vast rare earth deposit sought by US and Chinese firms, saying it is proceeding without an economic viability study.
The competition for the Mrima Hill deposit comes as Washington seeks alternatives to Chinese-dominated mineral supply chains. Kenya opened bidding for the coastal site in March, inviting companies to seek rights to develop its rare earths and niobium, a metal used in aerospace manufacturing.
In a post on X on Sunday, opposition Wiper Patriotic Front spokesperson Ndegwa Njiru questioned the tender, saying the government has no “economic viability report or bankable feasibility study” for the $62 billion project.
The tender document acknowledges that no economic viability report has been prepared, but says the initial invitation for expressions of interest does not constitute a mining contract.
The government has not published an estimated cost for developing the mine and processing plant. The widely cited $62 billion figure comes from a 2013 estimate of minerals in the ground by former license holder Cortec Mining Kenya, which was majority-owned by Canada’s Pacific Wildcat Resources.
Kenya revoked Cortec’s license that year, saying it had been issued irregularly without the approvals required to mine in a protected forest. The company later lost an international arbitration case challenging the decision.
Kenyan Mining Minister Hassan Ali Joho told Semafor on Monday that six companies, including firms from the US, China, and Australia, are competing for the license in the latest bidding round. US-based Critical Metals Corp has said its Mrima Earth consortium was shortlisted. Earlier reporting also named US firm ReElement and China’s Jinan Yuxiao among the contenders.
Nairobi wants the successful bidder to process minerals in the East African nation as part of an effort to retain more of the value from the deposit instead of exporting raw materials. The government requires applicants to demonstrate that they can build an on-site processing plant.
Joho also said talks with the US on building refineries and processing plants in Kenya are at a “very advanced” stage and “intertwined” with the Mrima Hill bidding.
Earlier this month, US Assistant Secretary of State for African Affairs Frank Garcia pledged support for Kenya’s mineral processing industry. During talks in New York last week, Kenyan President William Ruto and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio discussed opportunities for American firms in the African country’s critical minerals sector.
Washington has made a similar push in DR Congo, the world’s largest cobalt producer. In December, the US signed a minerals partnership with Kinshasa alongside a peace agreement it brokered between Congo and Rwanda.
Congolese lawyers and rights advocates have challenged the minerals deal in court, arguing that it bypassed parliament and threatens national control over natural resources.
China, however, still dominates rare earth supply chains. The International Energy Agency said in April that the country accounts for more than 90% of global refining of the rare earths used in permanent magnets.

items.title: Holy See: Culture of responsibility needed to counter new forms of financial crime
items.summary: Archbishop Anthony Ekpo, Assessor for General Affairs of the Secretariat of State and President of the Financial Security Committee, speaks at an international conference at Rome’s Luiss University dedicated to legislation introduced 15 years ago in the Vatican to prevent and combat money laundering and terrorist financing: “The purpose of financial integrity is to safeguard trust in institutions.” Read all
items.body_text:
Holy See: Culture of responsibility needed to counter new forms of financial crime
By Daniele Piccini
Fifteen years after the introduction of the first law on the prevention and combating of money laundering and terrorist financing in the Vatican City State, âthe best way to honour this progress is not simply to celebrate it, but to subject it once again to careful scrutiny,â particularly in light of emerging forms of financial crime.
This was at the heart of the address which Archbishop Anthony Ekpo, Assessor for General Affairs of the Secretariat of State and President of the Financial Security Committee of the Holy See and the Vatican City State, delivered on the morning of September 29.
He spoke at The Dome at Romeâs Luiss University, which hosted an international day of study on the theme âFifteen Years Since the First Anti-Money Laundering (AML) / Countering the Financing of Terrorism (CFT) Law in the Holy See and the Vatican City State.â
Threat posed by new technologies
Efforts to review and strengthen the system are all the more necessary given the increasingly widespread use of new technologies in financial crime.
âThe next 15 years,â Archbishop Ekpo said, âwill bring risks that would have been difficult to imagine in 2010: increasingly complex financial technologies, instantaneous cross-border transactions, activities involving virtual assets, artificial intelligence and new forms of financial crime. We will certainly need strong laws, but also, above all, strong institutions, effective cooperation, professional judgment, technological expertise and a culture of responsibility.â
Pope Benedict XIV's initiative
The President of the Financial Security Committee recalled the timing, circumstances and reasons behind the introduction of the new legislation.
âOn December 30, 2010, Law No. 127 of the Vatican City State was promulgated, establishing the first comprehensive legal framework for the prevention and combating of money laundering and terrorist financing. On the same day, Pope Benedict XVI extended its application to the relevant institutions of the Holy See and decided to participate in an international system based on shared responsibility and mutual accountability.â
The years following the introduction of the new legislation saw the gradual development of a broader legal and institutional framework, Archbishop Ekpo continued, including âparticipation in the international system for combating money laundering through periodic external assessments and ongoing dialogue, while subsequent reforms strengthened prevention, supervision, financial intelligence, coordination and international cooperation.â
Pope Francis: Money must serve, not govern
Supervision, financial intelligence and international cooperation, he further argued, serve to âprotect peopleâ and âpreserve trust,â while ensuring that âfinancial resources remain what they should always beâmeans placed at the service of the legitimate purposes of institutions and individuals and, ultimately, the common good.â
While such transparency is important for every institution, it is indispensable for an institution such as the Vatican City State, which is entrusted with managing donations and funding for charitable purposes.
âThe resources entrusted to its institutions,â the President of the Financial Security Committee said, âhave a value that goes beyond the economicâthey carry an expectation of integrity and trust in the purpose for which they are made available and in the way they will be administered. In this sense, financial integrity is therefore inseparable from trust in institutions.â
This is a task of âprofound significance,â a principle Pope Francis clearly understood âwhen, upon receiving the evaluators of the anti-money laundering system in 2020 (Moneyval), he recalled a principle expressed in Evangelii gaudium: money must serve, not govern.â
15 years of progress

items.title: Cardinal Koch: Peace among Churches is a responsibility for Europe
items.summary: At a conference in Rome on “Religions and Diplomacy,” Cardinal Kurt Koch, Prefect of the Dicastery for Promoting Christian Unity, speaks to Vatican News about the responsibility of Churches in Europe to take responsibility for rediscovering unity and peace, so that they can help build it in society. Read all
items.body_text:
Cardinal Koch: Peace among Churches is a responsibility for Europe
By Maria Milvia Morciano
âFirst, we must rediscover peace within the Church and among all the Churches. Ecumenism can help us live in balance amid diversity.â
With these words, Cardinal Kurt Koch, Prefect of the Dicastery for Promoting Christian Unity, explained how Christiansâ first contribution to peace must be to seek greater unity and peace among the Churches themselves.
He said this in Rome at the conference âReligions and Diplomacy,â taking place from September 28 to 30 at Palazzo San Calisto, on the occasion of the 30th anniversary of the International Association Political Charity.
What can religions offer in the search for peace? What role can diplomacy play in resolving conflicts? These questions are at the heart of the initiative.
The presentation also pointed to a growing demand for moral reference points in public life, while scientific and technological developments are raising new questions for societies and governments.
The opening session also brought together diplomatic representatives accredited to the Holy See and Maria Angela Falà, former president of the Italian Buddhist Union.
A Europe that is more than its economy
The Cardinal began with a familiar image of the continent: the European Union, its institutions, the common market and the euro.
It is a decisive achievement, born in part from the determination to prevent a repetition of the wars that devastated Europe. Yet its identity does not end with its economic and political structures.
For Cardinal Koch, Europe is also a historical, spiritual and cultural reality, and this raises the question guiding his presentationâcan Europe have a future if it loses awareness of its origins? He also pointed to the relationship between the words âcultureâ and âworshipâ (culto), drawing attention to the religious dimension that has helped shape cultures, even though culture and worship are often regarded today as separate.
To understand Europeâs roots, he proposed the image of three hills: Golgotha in Jerusalem, the Acropolis in Athens and the Capitoline Hill in Rome. In them, he sees the encounter between the biblical heritage, Greek thought and the Roman legal tradition, echoing Pope Benedict XVI, who in his 2011 address to the Bundestag identified this encounter as one of the origins of European culture.
In the Greek heritage, the Prefect recognized the search for the good and the trueâa democracy, he observed, needs a law and a criterion of justice that do not depend solely on the will of the majority.
In encountering Greek philosophy, the Christian faith embraced the rational search for truth as part of its own history. Turning to ancient Rome, the Cardinal emphasized its legal tradition and its ability to bring Christianity and political power into dialogue, developments that also contributed to the distinction between Church and Stateâessential to freedom of conscience.
In his view, these roots concern more than the past. Europe is called to pass on three principles: reference to God, the dignity of the human person and social responsibility.
Human beings, he argued, cannot be understood as isolated individuals, because they realize their freedom through relationships with others. Cardinal Koch spoke of a profound weakening of respect for human life, which he connected to the loss of awareness of Godâs presence in public life.
Remembering Europeâs Christian roots, he clarified, does not mean asking for a privileged position for the Church, but recognizing a component of Europeâs cultural history and asking about its vitality today.
Peace also begins with the Churches
Asked what contribution the Churches can make when politics and diplomacy struggle to find a way forward, Cardinal Koch first turned his attention to the Christian world itself.
The starting point, he recalled, must be the misunderstandings, differences and polarization present today, adding the need to ârediscover peace among all

items.title: ‘Paying attention in age of clickbait’ – 2027 World Communications Day theme
items.summary: The Vatican Dicastery for Communication releases the theme for the 2027 World Communications Day, which is “A New Gaze: Paying Attention in the Age of Clickbait.” Read all
items.body_text:
âPaying attention in age of clickbaitâ â 2027 World Communications Day theme
By Devin Watkins
On the feast of St. Gabriel the Archangel, the Holy Seeâs Dicastery for Communication released the theme for the 61st World Communications Day.
The theme will be âA New Gaze: Paying Attention in the Age of Clickbait,â according to a press release published on Tuesday by the Dicastery (our parent organization).
This yearâs theme invites Christians to open ourselves to âa conversion of our gaze: to look again, with attention and with love.â
âThe attention economy, with its struggle for a few moments of interest amid the rapid and endless flow of content, is transforming not only our cognitive abilities but also the depth of our interpersonal communication,â it noted.
Only by paying attention to others with love can we see the âworld, others, even ourselves, as Christ sees us: called by name and loved.â
âOur communication changes when our gaze chooses to encounter others rather than judge them,â said the statement.
People are inundated every moment of every day with expectations of rapid reactions and superficial relationships, resulting in a lack of genuine attention fueled by digital culture, it added.
âYet attention is a precious form of generosity: the word âattentionâ comes from ad-tendereâto reach out toward the other and toward the truth,â said the press release. âChristian communication can rediscover attention as both a gift and a way of seeingâthe gaze of Jesus, who saw and allowed Himself to be touched.â
Rather than seeking to capture attention, communicating is about safeguarding attention âas a precious resource for relationships.â
In our modern age of âclickbait,â Christians are invited to pay attention and rediscover a healthy form of attention to one another.
âCommunication is not just about words,â concluded the press release. âIt involves the entire person and asks us to look, hear, and feel again in order to answer Christâs call.â
World Communications Day 2027 takes place in many parts of the worldâincluding the United States, England and Wales, France, Spain, Poland, and Italyâon May 9, but is celebrated on different days in various parts of the world, as set by the national Bishopsâ Conferences.
